title: The body's organ systems
description: The body works as 11 organ systems, each a group of organs sharing a major job: wrapping and moving, supplying and cleaning, controlling and defending.

facts.text: Anatomy textbooks such as OpenStax's count 11 organ systems in the human body; an organ system is a group of organs that work together on a major body function.
The integumentary system (skin, hair and nails) encloses the body, the skeletal system supports it, and the muscular system moves it along with the skeleton and helps keep it warm.

The respiratory system brings in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide, the digestive system processes food, the cardiovascular system (heart and blood vessels) delivers oxygen and nutrients, and the urinary system removes waste from the blood and balances water.

The nervous system senses and responds, the endocrine system sends hormones that regulate the body, the lymphatic system returns fluid to the blood and defends against germs, and the reproductive system makes sex cells.

title: Systems work as a team
description: No organ system works alone: breathing and circulation share oxygen delivery, nerves, bones and muscles share movement, and muscles and blood share keeping warm.

facts.text: The respiratory system delivers oxygen to the blood, and the cardiovascular system carries oxygen and nutrients on to the body's tissues.
The nervous system detects and processes sensory information and activates the body's responses; the skeletal system supports the body and, with the muscular system, enables movement.
The muscular system helps maintain body temperature, and the cardiovascular system helps even out temperature across the body.

title: What a cell is
description: Cells are the basic building blocks of all living things; each takes in nutrients, makes energy and does a job, and the body is made of trillions.

facts.text: Cells are the basic building blocks of all living things, and the human body is made of trillions of them.

Cells provide structure for the body, take in nutrients from food, convert those nutrients into energy and carry out specialized functions; they also contain the body's hereditary material and can make copies of themselves.

title: The main parts of a cell
description: A cell has a plasma membrane that controls what enters and leaves, jelly-like cytoplasm, a nucleus that directs the cell, and mitochondria that supply energy.

facts.text: The plasma membrane is the cell's outer lining: it separates the cell from its surroundings and lets materials enter and leave.
The cytoplasm is the jelly-like fluid, and the structures in it, that fills the cell around the nucleus.
The nucleus is the cell's command center, sending directions that tell the cell to grow, mature, divide or die.
Mitochondria convert energy from food into a form the cell can use; they generate most of the chemical energy that powers the cell.

title: How many cells make a body
description: A 2016 estimate puts a reference adult at about 30 trillion human cells, most of them red blood cells; counts vary with body size.

facts.text: A 2016 estimate by Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo put the number of human cells in a "reference man" (aged 20 to 30, 70 kg, 170 cm tall) at about 30 trillion.
Sender, Fuchs and Milo did not count cells one by one; they combined published estimates of the number of each cell type, such as red blood cells and platelets, and added them up.
Red blood cells make up about 84 percent of all human cells by number.
Counting 30 trillion cells at one per second, without stopping, would take about 950,000 years (30 trillion seconds).

A 2023 study by Ian Hatton and colleagues estimated about 36 trillion cells in a reference man, 28 trillion in a reference woman and 17 trillion in a 10-year-old child, so counts differ with body size.

title: How many kinds of cell
description: The body's cells fall into about 400 types whose masses span seven orders of magnitude: red blood cells lead the count, muscle cells the mass.

facts.text: The 2023 Hatton study sorted the body's cells into about 400 cell types.
Human cell masses span about seven orders of magnitude, from red blood cells to the largest muscle fibers, comparable to the difference between a shrew and a blue whale.
Skeletal muscle cells make up about half of the body's cell mass, even though they are only a tiny fraction of its cells.

title: The four tissue types
description: The body has four main tissue types: epithelial covers and lines, connective binds and supports, muscle contracts, and nervous tissue carries signals.

facts.text: There are four main tissue types: epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines passages, connective tissue binds and supports, muscle tissue contracts to make movement, and nervous tissue sends signals between body parts.
The stomach wall has an epithelial lining, connective tissue, three layers of smooth muscle that churn food, and networks of nerves.

title: Levels of organization
description: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and the systems together make the organism.

facts.text: The body is organized in levels: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and the organ systems make up the whole organism.
A tissue is a group of many similar cells that work together to perform a specific function.
An organ is a distinct structure made of two or more tissue types that performs one or more specific functions.

title: DNA, the instruction book
description: DNA is the hereditary material, written in four chemical letters (A, C, G, T) whose order carries information; about 3 billion letters, over 99 percent shared.

facts.text: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the hereditary material in humans and almost all other organisms.
DNA stores information as a code of four chemical bases, A, C, G and T, and their order carries the information, much as letters in order form words and sentences.
Human DNA is about 3 billion bases long, and more than 99 percent of those bases are the same in all people.
DNA's two strands twist into a double helix, like a spiral ladder whose rungs are base pairs: A with T and C with G.

title: Where the body keeps DNA
description: Nearly every cell holds the same DNA, mostly in the nucleus as 46 chromosomes, with a little in mitochondria; mature red blood cells have no nucleus.

facts.text: If all the DNA from a single human cell were stretched out end to end, it would be about six feet (about 2 meters) long, yet it fits in a nucleus visible only with a specialized microscope.
Nearly every cell in a person's body has the same DNA.
Most DNA is in the cell nucleus, but a small amount is found in the mitochondria.
Human DNA is packaged into 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs.
Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus.

title: What a gene is
description: A gene is a stretch of DNA; about 20,000 human genes code for proteins, filling under 2 percent of the genome, and most traits involve many genes.

facts.text: A gene is the basic unit of heredity, a stretch of DNA; some genes are instructions for making proteins, and many others help control other genes.
Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes.
The information for the roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes takes up less than 2 percent of the human genome (NHGRI estimates about 1.5 percent).
Traits like height are shaped by hundreds of gene variants, each with a small effect, plus environmental factors such as nutrition.

title: From gene to protein
description: A gene is copied into messenger RNA, which leaves the nucleus; a ribosome reads it three letters at a time and links amino acids into a protein.

facts.text: Proteins do most of the work in cells and are needed for the structure, function and regulation of the body's tissues and organs.
Some proteins are enzymes that carry out chemical reactions, some are messengers that carry signals between cells, and some give cells structure and support.
Proteins are chains built from 20 kinds of amino acids, linked like pearls on a necklace; their order sets each protein's shape and job.

Making a protein takes two steps: in transcription a gene is copied into messenger RNA, which carries the message out of the nucleus; in translation a ribosome in the cytoplasm reads it and links amino acids into a protein.
A ribosome reads messenger RNA three letters at a time; each three-letter codon usually codes for one amino acid.

title: How much of the body is water
description: Water is about 75 percent of a newborn and 50 to 60 percent of an adult, less in old age and with more fat; almost two-thirds of it is inside cells.

facts.text: Water makes up about 75 percent of body mass in infants, about 50 to 60 percent in adults, and can fall to about 45 percent in old age.
Body water share changes because the mix of tissues changes over a lifetime; fat tissue holds less water than lean tissue, so people with more body fat have a lower percentage of water.
Almost two-thirds of the body's water is inside cells, where it is the main component of the cytoplasm; the other third is outside cells, around them and in the blood.

title: What water does in the body
description: Water keeps temperature normal (evaporating sweat cools the skin), cushions joints, protects the spinal cord and carries waste away.

facts.text: Water helps the body keep a normal temperature, lubricate and cushion joints, protect the spinal cord and other sensitive tissues, and get rid of waste.
When sweat evaporates, it cools the skin; sweating is an important way the body sheds heat in hot weather and during physical activity.

title: The microbes that live on you
description: Trillions of microbes, mostly gut bacteria of more than 10,000 species, live on and in the body; they help digest food and make vitamins.

facts.text: The microbes that live on and in the human body, including bacteria, are together called the human microbiome, which the NIH studied in its Human Microbiome Project.
Almost all of the body's bacteria, about 38 trillion, live in the colon; bacteria elsewhere in the body add up to far fewer.
Gut microbes break down proteins, fats and carbohydrates in food into nutrients we can absorb, and make beneficial compounds such as vitamins that our own genome cannot produce.
More than 10,000 microbial species live in the human body, according to the NIH Human Microbiome Project.
The human microbiome carries about 8 million unique protein-coding genes, hundreds of times more than the human genome.

title: Bacteria and human cells, about one to one
description: A 2016 recount found about 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells, roughly one to one, weighing about 0.2 kg; a bowel movement can tip the ratio.

facts.text: The 2016 Sender, Fuchs and Milo estimate put the bacteria in a reference man at about 38 trillion, about 1.3 for every human cell: roughly one to one.
For decades, textbooks claimed bacteria vastly outnumbered human cells; the figure came from a rough back-of-the-envelope estimate made in the 1970s.
All the bacteria in the body weigh only about 0.2 kg in total.
Each bowel movement removes roughly a quarter to a third of the colon's bacteria, enough to tip the ratio toward human cells for a while.

title: Vesalius and human dissection
description: Galen's anatomy, drawn from animals, ruled into the 1500s; in 1543 Vesalius published anatomy from human dissections he did himself and corrected Galen.

facts.text: Galen, a Greek physician in the Roman Empire (129 to about 216 CE), learned anatomy by dissecting animals such as apes and pigs, because dissecting human bodies was taboo.
Galen's books on anatomy were still treated as authoritative in medical education in the 1500s, more than a thousand years after he wrote them.
In 1543 Andreas Vesalius published On the Structure of the Human Body (De humani corporis fabrica), based on human dissections he did himself; it was more accurate than any earlier description.
Galen said the human lower jaw is made of two bones, which is true of a dog; Vesalius showed that the human jaw is a single bone.

title: Microscopes and cell theory
description: Hooke named cells in cork (1665), Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria in his own tooth plaque (1683), and by the late 1830s cell theory said all life is made of cells.

facts.text: In his 1665 book Micrographia, Robert Hooke coined the word "cell" for the box-like structures he saw in cork through a lens.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see bacteria; in 1683 he described "little animalcules" in the plaque from his own teeth.
Leeuwenhoek made microscopes with a single lens he ground himself, magnifying up to about 300 times.
By the late 1830s, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann proposed cell theory: all living things are made of cells, and the cell is the basic unit of life.

title: The body renews its cells
description: About 330 billion cells, roughly 1 percent, are replaced every day, mostly blood cells; each new cell comes from an existing one and gets a full copy of the DNA.

facts.text: A 2021 estimate by Ron Sender and Ron Milo found that about 330 billion cells, roughly 1 percent of the body's cells, are replaced every day.
Replacing about 330 billion cells a day works out to about 3.8 million new cells every second.
About 90 percent of the cells replaced each day, by number, are blood cells.
New cells arise from existing cells, one of the principles of cell theory.
When a cell divides, each new cell needs an exact copy of the old cell's DNA, and each of DNA's two strands serves as a pattern for the copy.

title: How many bones an adult has
description: An adult skeleton has 206 bones: 80 in the axial skeleton and 126 in the appendicular skeleton, with 106 of them in the hands and feet.

facts.text: The adult human skeleton has 206 bones.

Each hand has 27 bones (8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges) and each foot has 26 (7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges), so the hands and feet hold 106 of the adult's 206 bones, leaving 100 for the rest of the skeleton.

The axial skeleton (80 bones: skull, spine and rib cage) protects the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs; the appendicular skeleton (126 bones) is the limbs plus the bones that attach them to the axial skeleton.

title: What the skeleton does
description: The skeleton supports the body, anchors muscles for movement, protects organs, makes blood cells in red marrow, stores fat in yellow marrow and banks minerals such as calcium.

facts.text: The skeleton supports the body, lets it move by giving muscles attachment points, protects internal organs, produces blood cells in red marrow, and stores minerals (especially calcium and phosphorus) and fat.
About 99 percent of the body's calcium is held in the bones (and teeth).

title: What bone is made of
description: Bone is living tissue: flexible collagen fibers hardened with calcium phosphate crystals, arranged as dense compact bone outside and a lattice of spongy bone inside.

facts.text: Bone is a living, metabolically active connective tissue made of bone cells in a mineralized matrix.
Bone's two main materials are collagen, whose fibers make it flexible rather than brittle, and calcium phosphate crystals (hydroxyapatite), which make it hard and strong.
Compact bone is the denser, stronger bone tissue on the outside; spongy bone inside is a lattice of thin struts called trabeculae with open spaces, and the struts form along lines of stress.

title: Marrow, the blood factory
description: Red marrow, in the spaces of spongy bone such as in the hip and thigh bones, makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets; yellow marrow is mostly fat.

facts.text: Red marrow fills spaces in some spongy bone, for example in the hip and thigh bones, and makes the blood cells: red blood cells that carry oxygen, white blood cells that fight infection and platelets that help blood clot.
Yellow marrow is mostly fat tissue, which can serve as an energy store.

title: Joints sorted by how much they move
description: A joint is where bones meet; joints can be immovable (skull sutures), slightly movable (between vertebrae) or freely movable (synovial joints).

facts.text: A joint is any place where two bones (or bone and cartilage) meet and connect.
By movement, joints are immovable (like the sutures joining skull bones, which protect the brain), slightly movable (like the discs between vertebrae) or freely movable (synovial joints).

title: How freely movable joints work
description: Synovial joints cap bone ends with cartilage inside a capsule of lubricating synovial fluid; their shape (hinge, pivot, ball-and-socket) sets how they move.

facts.text: In a synovial joint, the bone ends are covered with smooth articular cartilage inside a capsule whose lining makes synovial fluid, a thick, slippery fluid that lubricates the joint and reduces friction.

Hinge joints (elbow, knee, ankle) bend and straighten along one axis; a pivot joint between the top two vertebrae lets the head rotate; the hip and shoulder are the only ball-and-socket joints and have the greatest range of motion.

title: Fractures and how doctors see them
description: A fracture is a break in a bone; X-rays show it because calcium-rich bone absorbs X-rays, and a cast or splint keeps the bone still so it heals in line.

facts.text: A fracture is a break in a bone, usually caused by an injury such as a fall, car accident or sports injury; overuse and repetitive motions can also cause fractures.
Bones contain calcium, which absorbs X-rays readily, so bone shows up white on an X-ray while muscle and fat appear in shades of gray.
A healing bone keeps whatever position it is in, so a bone not set back in line heals deformed; a cast or splint keeps the bone from moving while it heals.

title: How a broken bone heals
description: A break heals in stages: a clot within hours, a cartilage callus within days, spongy bone over weeks, then remodeling into compact bone over months to years, faster in children.

facts.text: Within hours of a fracture, blood clots around the break (about 6 to 8 hours); within about 48 hours a callus of cartilage starts bridging the gap; bone cells then replace the cartilage with spongy bone; finally compact bone forms and remodeling often leaves no trace of the break.
The clot forms over hours to days, the callus over days to weeks, and remodeling takes months to years; children go through the same stages much faster than adults.

title: The three kinds of muscle
description: Skeletal muscle is attached to bones and voluntary; smooth muscle lines hollow organs and is involuntary; cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and is involuntary.

facts.text: Skeletal muscle is attached to bones, voluntary and striated; smooth muscle lines hollow organs such as blood vessels, the gut and the bladder, and is involuntary and unstriated; cardiac muscle, only in the heart wall, is involuntary and striated.
Skeletal muscle depends completely on signals from the nervous system to contract, while the heart and smooth muscle can work without conscious control.

title: Muscles only pull, so they work in pairs
description: A muscle can only contract and pull, so muscles work in opposing pairs: the biceps bends the elbow and the triceps straightens it.

facts.text: Muscles can only contract, so they pull and never push; they work in opposing (antagonistic) pairs, and when one contracts, its partner relaxes.
The biceps bends (flexes) the elbow and the triceps on the back of the arm straightens (extends) it; the quadriceps straighten the knee and the hamstrings bend it.

title: Sliding filaments
description: Inside a muscle fiber, myosin heads grab thin actin filaments and pull them past thick filaments, re-cocking with ATP energy after each short pull.

facts.text: A muscle fiber contracts when myosin heads on the thick filaments grab the thin actin filaments and pull them, sliding them past the thick filaments; this is the sliding filament model.
Each myosin head pulls only a very short distance, then lets go and is re-cocked using energy from ATP before it grabs and pulls again.

title: What tendons and ligaments connect
description: Tendons connect muscle to bone and carry its pull; ligaments connect bone to bone at a joint; the Achilles tendon is the thickest.

facts.text: Tendons connect muscle to bone, carrying a muscle's pull to the skeleton; ligaments connect bones to each other at a joint.
Some ligaments contain elastic fibers as well as collagen, which lets them return to their original length after stretching.

The Achilles tendon, which connects the calf muscles to the heel, is the thickest and most powerful tendon in the body; it is named after the Greek mythical hero Achilles, whose heel was his only vulnerable spot.

title: Why tendons and ligaments are strong but slow to heal
description: Tendons and ligaments are dense connective tissue of parallel collagen fibers that resist stretching; with little blood supply, they heal slowly. A sprain hurts a ligament; a strain, a muscle or tendon.

facts.text: Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue: tough collagen fibers lined up in parallel, which resist stretching in the direction of the pull.
Tendons do not have an abundant blood supply, so they heal slowly.
A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament; a strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon.

title: How muscles grow stronger
description: Muscles grow without making new cells: resistance exercise adds myofibrils, the bundles of actin and myosin filaments, so each fiber gets thicker (hypertrophy).

facts.text: Muscles grow without forming new cells: resistance exercise makes fibers build more myofibrils (structural proteins), so each fiber gets thicker; this is called hypertrophy.
A myofibril is a chain of many sarcomeres, the units that hold the thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments; myofibrils contract as their sarcomeres contract.

title: Endurance changes and disuse
description: Endurance exercise can add mitochondria and capillaries to muscle; a muscle that is not used loses structural proteins and shrinks (atrophy), which exercise can often reverse.

facts.text: Endurance exercise can increase the number of mitochondria in muscle cells and the density of capillaries, the tiny blood vessels, in the muscle.
When a muscle is not used, it loses structural proteins and its mass decreases (atrophy); atrophy from disuse can often be reversed with exercise.

title: Why babies have more bones
description: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones (sources vary); many start as cartilage, and over childhood separate pieces fuse, from skull bones to the hip bones and sacrum, into the adult 206.

facts.text: Estimates of the bones in a newborn vary from about 270 to about 300; as the skeleton grows, many of them fuse, leaving the adult 206.
Many of a baby's bones start as cartilage, a tough but flexible tissue; the cartilage is not turned into bone but serves as a template that bone replaces.

At birth the skull bones are not yet joined, which lets the skull change shape in the birth canal; the gaps, called fontanelles, allow brain growth. The one at the back usually closes by 1 to 2 months and the one at the front within 7 to 19 months.
Each hip bone forms from three bones (the ilium, ischium and pubis) that fuse during the late teenage years, and the sacrum is five vertebrae fused into one bone.

title: Growth plates
description: Long bones lengthen at growth plates, layers of cartilage near their ends that are turned into bone; when bone replaces the plate in early adulthood, growth in length stops.

facts.text: Long bones grow in length at growth plates (epiphyseal plates), layers of cartilage near each end: cartilage forms on one side and is replaced by bone on the other. Growth continues until early adulthood, when bone replaces the plate and only a thin line remains.

title: Bones and muscles as levers
description: Bones are levers, joints are fulcrums and muscles supply the effort; most arrangements, like the bent arm, trade force for a large, fast movement.

facts.text: The skeleton and muscles work as levers: bones are the stiff levers, joints are the fulcrums (pivots), contracting muscles supply the effort, and the load is whatever is moved, even the head when you lift it.

A bent arm is a Class 3 lever: the elbow is the pivot and the biceps pulls on the forearm closer to the elbow than the load; the muscle must pull harder than the load, but a small contraction gives a large, fast movement. Many muscle and bone combinations work this way.

title: The heart's four chambers
description: The heart is a fist-sized muscular pump with four chambers: atria receive blood, ventricles pump it; the right side sends blood to the lungs, the left side to the whole body.

facts.text: The heart is a muscular organ about the size of your fist that pumps blood through the body.
The heart has four chambers: two upper chambers, the right and left atria, which receive blood, and two lower chambers, the right and left ventricles, which pump blood out.
Oxygen-poor blood from the body enters the right atrium through two large veins, the venae cavae; the right ventricle then pumps it to the lungs.
Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, and the left ventricle generates the high pressure needed to pump it to the whole body.

title: Heart valves keep blood moving one way
description: Four valves open to let blood through and close to stop it flowing backward; their closing makes the lub-dub sound.

facts.text: The heart has four valves (tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary and aortic) that open to let blood through and close to stop it flowing backward.
The "lub" of a heartbeat is the sound of the mitral and tricuspid valves closing, and the "dub" is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing.

title: Heart rate and the heart's pacemaker
description: Each beat starts at the SA node in the right atrium; a normal resting adult rate is 60 to 100 beats a minute, faster in young children and during exercise.

facts.text: Your pulse is your heart rate, the number of heartbeats per minute, and you can feel it where an artery passes close to the skin, such as the wrist or the side of the neck.
Each heartbeat starts with an electrical signal from pacemaker cells in the sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium, and the signal makes the heart muscle contract.
At rest, a heart rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute is normal for adults and children aged 10 and older, and the heart beats faster during exercise.
Young children have faster resting heart rates (80 to 130 beats per minute at ages 1 to 2), while well-trained athletes can rest at 40 to 60.

title: How much the heart pumps
description: About 70 mL per beat, about 100,000 beats and 7,000 to 8,000 liters a day, nearly 2.9 billion beats and more than 200 million liters over 79 years.

facts.text: At rest, each beat of an adult heart pushes about 70 milliliters of blood out of a ventricle, and the heart moves about 5 liters a minute.
A heart beats about 100,000 times a day and pumps about 7,000 to 8,000 liters (about 2,000 gallons) of blood a day.
At about 100,000 beats a day, a heart beats nearly 2.9 billion times over an average life span of almost 79 years.
At 7,000 to 8,000 liters a day, a heart pumps more than 200 million liters of blood over 79 years (about 202 to 231 million).

title: Arteries and veins
description: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and have thick, elastic walls; veins carry it back at low pressure, with thinner walls, valves, and about two-thirds of the blood.

facts.text: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins return blood to the heart.
Arteries have thicker walls than veins, and the large arteries near the heart are elastic, stretching as the ventricles push blood in and then recoiling.
Veins carry blood at much lower pressure, so their walls are thinner, and many veins, especially in the limbs, have valves that keep blood flowing one way.
At any moment, the veins hold roughly two-thirds of the body's blood (about 64 percent, by one textbook estimate).
The pulmonary arteries carry blood that is low in oxygen from the heart's right ventricle to the lungs.

title: Capillaries, where delivery happens
description: Capillaries link the smallest arteries to the smallest veins; they are so narrow red cells pass single file, and their thin walls let oxygen, nutrients and wastes cross.

facts.text: Capillaries are the tiny vessels that link the smallest arteries to the smallest veins.
Most capillaries are about 8 to 10 micrometers wide, only wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file.
Capillary walls are a single thin layer of cells, and through them oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between the blood and the tissues.

title: What blood is made of
description: Blood is over half plasma, which is about 92 percent water, plus red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets; an adult has about 4 to 6 liters.

facts.text: When a blood sample is spun in a centrifuge it separates into layers: plasma on top, a thin pale layer of white blood cells and platelets, and red blood cells at the bottom.
Blood is made of a liquid part, plasma, plus red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
Plasma makes up over half of blood's volume, and it is about 92 percent water, with salts and proteins dissolved in it.
An adult has about 4 to 6 liters of blood, roughly 8 percent of body weight.
White blood cells fight infection, and platelets help blood clot when you have a cut; together they make up less than 1 percent of a blood sample.

title: Red blood cells carry oxygen
description: Red blood cells, about 45 percent of blood's volume, carry oxygen on hemoglobin, the iron-containing protein that makes blood red; oxygen-rich blood is bright red, oxygen-poor blood dusky red.

facts.text: Red blood cells deliver oxygen from the lungs to the tissues; hemoglobin, an iron-containing protein, carries the oxygen and gives blood its red color.
Red blood cells make up about 45 percent of blood's volume.
Blood that has just picked up oxygen is bright red; blood that has given up oxygen in the tissues is a darker, dusky red.

title: ABO blood types
description: Landsteiner published the ABO groups in 1901 after seeing red cells clump when blood was mixed; your type depends on A and B antigens on red cell membranes.

facts.text: Blood transfusions were risky until Karl Landsteiner, an Austrian physician, discovered the major human blood groups.
In 1901 Karl Landsteiner published his discovery of the ABO blood groups, after finding that mixing blood from two people could make the red blood cells clump together.
Landsteiner received the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the human blood groups.
Your ABO type depends on two markers, the A and B antigens, on the plasma membrane of your red blood cells: type A has A, type B has B, type AB has both and type O has neither.
Plasma naturally carries antibodies against the ABO antigen or antigens a person lacks: type A blood has anti-B, type B has anti-A, type O has both and type AB has neither.

title: Why transfusions must match
description: Antibodies attack donated red cells carrying a marker the recipient lacks; Rh is a second label; O negative can go to anyone in an emergency and AB positive can receive any type.

facts.text: In a mismatched transfusion, the recipient's antibodies attach to the donated red blood cells, making them clump together and break apart.
Blood is also Rh positive or Rh negative, depending on whether red cells carry the Rh D antigen; about 85 percent of Americans are Rh positive.
Type O negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh D antigen, so they can be given to people of any type in an emergency; type AB positive people can receive red cells of any type.

title: What blood pressure measures
description: Blood pressure is the force of blood on artery walls, read as systolic (as the heart pumps) over diastolic (between beats), in mm Hg.

facts.text: Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries.
A blood pressure reading has two numbers: systolic, the pressure as the heart pumps blood out, over diastolic, the pressure between beats as the heart refills, both in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg).

title: Blood pressure categories and why it is checked
description: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline keeps four categories (normal, elevated, stage 1, stage 2); high blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so measuring is the only way to know.

facts.text: Under the 2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, normal is below 120/80 mm Hg; elevated is 120 to 129 systolic with diastolic below 80; stage 1 hypertension is 130 to 139 systolic or 80 to 89 diastolic; stage 2 is 140 or higher systolic or 90 or higher diastolic.
High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms until it leads to serious health problems, about 1 in 3 U.S. adults who have it don't know it, and measuring is the only way to know.
Over time, uncontrolled high blood pressure can lead to heart attack, heart failure, stroke and kidney disease.

title: Harvey shows that blood circulates
description: Galen said the liver makes blood that the body uses up; in 1628 Harvey showed by arithmetic and a tied-off arm that the same blood circulates, pumped by the heart.

facts.text: Before Harvey, physicians followed Galen's teaching that blood is made in the liver and flows out to the body, where it is used up; Harvey's idea challenged about 1,500 years of established belief.
In 1628 William Harvey, an English physician, published De Motu Cordis, arguing that the heart pumps the blood around the body in a continuous circuit.

Using cautious estimates of how much blood each beat pushes out, Harvey calculated that the heart pumps far more blood in a day than the whole body weighs, too much for the body to make from food and use up.
Harvey tied a band around a person's upper arm so the forearm veins swelled and showed their valves; blood in those veins could be pushed toward the heart but not away from it.
Harvey's theory was opposed by conservative physicians at first but was well established by the time he died.

title: Malpighi finds the missing link
description: Harvey could not see how blood crossed from arteries to veins; in 1661 Malpighi's microscope revealed the capillaries connecting them.

facts.text: Harvey could not see how blood passed from arteries to veins; capillaries were unknown in his time and confirmed later, after the microscope came into use.
In 1661 Marcello Malpighi, studying lung tissue under the microscope, described the network of capillaries connecting small arteries with small veins.

title: How blood clots
description: To stop bleeding, the vessel narrows, platelets form a plug, and clotting factors build a fibrin mesh; in hemophilia a missing clotting factor stops blood clotting properly.

facts.text: Stopping bleeding (hemostasis) takes three steps: the injured blood vessel narrows, platelets form a plug, and the blood clots (coagulation).
At a damaged vessel, platelets become spiky and sticky, bind to the exposed vessel wall and clump together into a plug.
Clotting factors, proteins in the blood, work with platelets to build a clot: a tough mesh of fibrin threads that holds the plug in place.
In hemophilia, an inherited bleeding disorder, the blood lacks enough of a clotting factor (factor VIII or IX), so it does not clot properly.

title: How a cut heals
description: After a clot and scab, a wound is swollen for 2 to 5 days while white cells fight germs, fills with new tissue over about 3 weeks, and leaves a smaller, weaker scar.

facts.text: Blood usually starts to clot within a few minutes or less, and the clot dries into a scab that protects the tissue underneath from germs.
For about 2 to 5 days the wound may be slightly swollen, red and tender as blood vessels open to bring oxygen and nutrients, and white blood cells fight germs and begin the repair.
Over about 3 weeks, the body repairs broken blood vessels and fills the wound with new tissue.
The scar that forms is smaller than the original wound and less strong and flexible than the skin around it.

title: Coronary arteries and heart attacks
description: The heart muscle is fed by the coronary arteries; in coronary heart disease plaque narrows them, and a sudden blockage of blood to part of the heart muscle is a heart attack.

facts.text: The heart muscle gets its own supply of oxygen-rich blood through the coronary arteries.
In coronary heart disease, the most common type of heart disease, fatty deposits called plaque build up and narrow the coronary arteries, so less oxygen-rich blood reaches the heart muscle.
A heart attack happens when the blood flow bringing oxygen to part of the heart muscle is suddenly blocked; if flow is not restored quickly, that part of the muscle begins to die.

title: What public-health bodies say affects heart health
description: The WHO calls cardiovascular diseases the leading cause of death, mostly preventable by addressing risks like unhealthy diet, inactivity, tobacco and alcohol; the AHA tracks eight measures in Life's Essential 8.

facts.text: The WHO reports that cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide, about a third of all deaths (an estimated 32 percent in 2022).

The WHO says most cardiovascular diseases can be prevented by addressing risk factors, and names the most important behavioral ones for heart disease and stroke as unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, tobacco use and harmful use of alcohol.

The American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 lists eight measures of heart health: eating better, being more active, quitting tobacco, getting healthy sleep, and managing weight, cholesterol, blood sugar and blood pressure.
In 2022 the AHA added sleep to its earlier list of seven measures, renaming it Life's Essential 8.

title: One lap of the circulation
description: Blood runs two circuits, through the lungs and through the body, passing the heart twice per lap; at rest the heart pumps about an adult's whole blood supply each minute.

facts.text: Blood travels in two circuits: the right side of the heart pumps it through the lungs and back to the left side, and the left side pumps it through the body and back to the right side, so one full lap passes through the heart twice.
At rest the heart pumps about 5 liters a minute, roughly an adult's whole blood supply, so on average your blood passes through the heart about once a minute.

title: Why cells need oxygen
description: Cells use oxygen to release energy from food, mostly in their mitochondria, and give off carbon dioxide as waste that the blood carries to the lungs to be breathed out.

facts.text: In cellular respiration, cells combine oxygen with molecules from food to release their energy, giving off carbon dioxide and water as waste; most of it takes place in the mitochondria.

Cells need oxygen to make the body's energy; the carbon dioxide they make passes into the blood, which must get rid of it, and in the lungs it moves from the blood into the air sacs to be breathed out.

title: What changes between a breath in and a breath out
description: Air going in is about 21 percent oxygen; air leaving the air sacs still holds about 16 percent, plus 4 to 5 percent carbon dioxide, so the body keeps only part of each breath's oxygen. Adults breathe 12 to 18 times a minute at rest.

facts.text: Air is about 21 percent oxygen; the last part of a breath out, from the air sacs, holds about 16 percent oxygen and 4 to 5 percent carbon dioxide.
A healthy adult at rest breathes about 12 to 18 times a minute.
At 12 to 18 breaths a minute, an adult at rest takes roughly 17,000 to 26,000 breaths a day (12 x 1,440 = 17,280; 18 x 1,440 = 25,920).

title: The airways: from windpipe to bronchioles
description: Air travels past the voice box, down the windpipe and through the branching bronchial tree to thousands of bronchioles; the right lung has three lobes and the left two; cilia sweep mucus and trapped dirt up to the throat to be swallowed.

facts.text: Air enters through the nose or mouth, passes the voice box and goes down the windpipe; inside the lungs the bronchial tubes branch into thousands of thinner bronchioles, which end in clusters of tiny air sacs called alveoli.
Anatomists call the branching airways inside the lungs the bronchial tree.
The right lung is divided into three lobes and the left lung into two.
Air brings in debris and germs; cilia, tiny hairlike structures lining the airways, beat constantly and sweep mucus and trapped debris toward the throat, where it is swallowed.

title: The alveoli, where gas is exchanged
description: The lungs hold about 480 million tiny air sacs wrapped in capillaries; oxygen crosses their very thin walls into the blood and carbon dioxide crosses back.

facts.text: A 2004 study counted a mean of about 480 million alveoli in adult human lungs (range 274 to 790 million), with larger lungs having more.

Each air sac is wrapped in tiny blood vessels called capillaries; oxygen passes through the thin walls into the blood and carbon dioxide moves the other way, across a barrier about 0.5 micrometers thick.

title: How the diaphragm pulls air in
description: The dome-shaped diaphragm contracts and moves down, enlarging the chest; pressure in the lungs falls below the air outside, and air flows in, about 500 mL in a quiet breath.

facts.text: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that separates the chest from the abdomen; it is the main muscle used for breathing.
When the diaphragm contracts it moves down, enlarging the chest cavity, and the lungs expand into the space.
When the lungs expand, the pressure inside them drops below the air pressure outside; air flows from higher to lower pressure, so it flows in.
A normal quiet breath moves about 500 milliliters of air.

title: Breathing out: recoil at rest, muscles at work
description: At rest, breathing out is passive: the muscles relax and the elastic lungs recoil like a balloon. During activity the rib muscles and extra muscles help force air in and out.

facts.text: Normal breathing out is passive: the diaphragm and rib muscles relax and the elastic lungs recoil, deflating like an open balloon, with no energy needed to push air out.
The muscles between the ribs, the intercostals, help with breathing during physical activity, and forced breathing uses extra muscles to push air both in and out.

title: How the vocal folds make a voice
description: The larynx holds two vocal folds that stay open for breathing and snap together to vibrate as air blows past; throat, nose and mouth shape the sound, and tongue and lips make it speech.

facts.text: The larynx, or voice box, sits between the base of the tongue and the top of the windpipe (trachea).
Voice is made by the vocal folds (vocal cords), two bands of tissue in the larynx: they are open for breathing and snap together, vibrating as air from the lungs blows past, when you speak.
The sound travels through the throat, nose and mouth, which act as resonating spaces that shape it, and movements mainly of the tongue and lips turn it into speech.

title: What sets the pitch of a voice
description: Pitch is how fast the vocal folds vibrate, more than 100 times a second in speech; tightening them raises pitch like tuning a guitar string, and shorter, thinner folds give women and children higher voices.

facts.text: How fast the vocal folds vibrate sets the pitch of the voice; they vibrate more than 100 times a second when you speak, and changing their tension changes pitch, like tuning a guitar string.
Vocal folds are shorter and thinner in women and children, which partly explains their higher-pitched voices.

title: Coughs and sneezes clear the airways
description: Airway sensors detect irritants and trigger coughs and sneezes. A cough takes a deep breath, holds the glottis shut while muscles build pressure, then blasts air out; a sneeze bursts air through the nose and mouth.

facts.text: Sensors in the airways detect irritants and can trigger sneezing or coughing; coughing is a reflex that keeps the throat and airways clear.
A cough starts with a deep breath in; then the glottis, the gap between the vocal cords, stays shut while breathing-out muscles squeeze to build pressure, and it suddenly opens to blast air out.
A sneeze is a sudden, forceful, uncontrolled burst of air through the nose and mouth, usually set off by irritation of the lining of the nose or throat, for example by pollen, dust or a cold.

title: What a hiccup is
description: A hiccup is a spasm of the diaphragm that pulls in a sudden breath, cut off by the vocal cords snapping shut, which makes the 'hic'. Most bouts pass in minutes.

facts.text: A hiccup is an involuntary spasm of the diaphragm that pulls in a sudden breath, followed by a quick closing of the vocal cords that cuts it off and makes the 'hic' sound.
Hiccups often start for no clear reason and most often go away after a few minutes.

title: Why air is thinner up high
description: Air is about 21 percent oxygen at every altitude, but pressure falls with height, so each breath brings in less oxygen; at Everest's summit pressure is about 30 percent of sea level. Messner and Habeler first climbed it without bottled oxygen in 1978.

facts.text: The share of oxygen in air stays about 21 percent at every altitude, but air pressure falls with height, so each breath brings less oxygen into the lungs.
At the height of Everest's summit, air pressure is only about 30 percent of its sea-level value.
In 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler became the first to climb Everest without bottled (supplemental) oxygen.

title: How bodies adapt to altitude
description: Given time, the body acclimatizes: deeper, faster breathing, a faster heart and more red blood cells. Altitude sickness, usually above about 2,400 m, is more likely with a fast climb and usually fades in 2 to 5 days.

facts.text: The body acclimatizes to altitude by breathing more deeply and faster, raising heart rate, and over time making more red blood cells to carry oxygen.

Acute mountain sickness comes from lower air pressure and oxygen, usually above about 2,400 meters (8,000 feet); it is more likely the faster you climb, and symptoms usually fade within 2 to 5 days as the body acclimatizes.

title: Carbon dioxide drives the urge to breathe
description: A respiratory center in the brainstem runs breathing automatically; its main signal is rising carbon dioxide, which makes the brain more acidic. Low oxygen drives breathing only when it falls quite low.

facts.text: Breathing is usually automatic: a respiratory center in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem sets its rate, responding to carbon dioxide, oxygen and acidity (pH) in the blood.

The main signal to breathe is rising carbon dioxide, not falling oxygen: carbon dioxide makes the brain more acidic, which drives faster, deeper breathing, while low oxygen drives breathing only once it is quite low.

title: Why breath-holding in water is dangerous
description: Hyperventilating or long breath-holding lowers carbon dioxide, delaying the urge to breathe while oxygen keeps falling, which can cause blackout and drowning; CDC warns against it, and strong swimmers have died this way.

facts.text: Hyperventilating (overbreathing) or breath-holding before swimming lowers the body's carbon dioxide, delaying the urge to surface while oxygen keeps falling, which can cause loss of consciousness underwater.
The CDC warns that hyperventilating before swimming underwater, or holding your breath underwater for long periods, can cause you to pass out and drown.

A CDC report found 16 drowning incidents linked to dangerous underwater breath-holding in New York State from 1988 to 2011; all 4 people who died were advanced swimmers aged 17 to 22 who had hyperventilated on purpose.

title: How smoking damages the lungs
description: Smoke stalls and damages the airway cilia and adds mucus; smoking is the main US cause of COPD, including emphysema, which damages the walls between air sacs.

facts.text: Cigarette smoke paralyzes and damages the cilia that sweep the airways clean and makes the airways produce more mucus, slowing the clearing of mucus.

Cigarette smoking is the main cause of COPD in the US; COPD damages the airways or other parts of the lung, as in emphysema (damaged walls between air sacs) and chronic bronchitis (inflamed airway lining), and has no cure.

title: Smoking and lung cancer
description: In the US about 80 percent of lung cancer deaths are linked to smoking, and smokers are 15 to 30 times more likely to get or die from it; WHO says there is no safe level of tobacco exposure; risk falls after quitting.

facts.text: In the US, cigarette smoking is linked to about 80 percent of lung cancer deaths, and people who smoke are 15 to 30 times more likely to get or die from lung cancer than people who don't.
The WHO states that all forms of tobacco use are harmful and there is no safe level of exposure, and the CDC says smoke from other people's cigarettes also causes lung cancer.
A person's risk of lung cancer goes down after they quit smoking.

title: What happens in the airways in asthma
description: Asthma is a long-term airway condition, the most common chronic disease in children. In an attack the airways swell, narrow, make extra mucus and may tighten, set off by triggers like pollen, smoke, cold air, infections or exercise.

facts.text: Asthma is a long-term (chronic) condition of the airways in the lungs; it has no cure but can be managed.
In an asthma attack the airways become inflamed, swell and narrow and can make extra mucus, and the muscles around them may tighten, making it harder to breathe, especially out.
People describe an asthma attack as like trying to suck air in through a straw, often with coughing, wheezing and a tight chest.
Things such as pollen, dust, smoke, fumes, cold air, viral infections and exercise can set off or worsen asthma symptoms.
Asthma is the most common chronic disease among children.

title: How asthma is managed with medical care
description: Asthma is managed with a healthcare provider and a written action plan; inhalers deliver medicine straight to the lungs, with quick-relief medicines opening airways in an attack and daily controllers reducing inflammation.

facts.text: Inhalers deliver asthma medicine directly to the lungs: quick-relief medicines open narrowed airways during an attack, and daily controller medicines reduce inflammation to help prevent attacks.
People with asthma work with a healthcare provider on a written asthma action plan that sets out which medicines to take and when.

title: The nose conditions the air
description: The nose (and mouth) warms and moistens incoming air, because cold, dry air irritates the lungs, and nostril hairs and the airways remove debris and germs.

facts.text: The nose and mouth warm and moisten incoming air, because cold, dry air can irritate the lungs.
Hairs just inside the nostrils block large debris such as dirt, and the airways work to remove debris and germs from incoming air.

title: The route through the digestive tract
description: Food travels one tube, mouth, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestine, anus, while the liver, pancreas and gallbladder add juices; the small intestine absorbs most nutrients and the large intestine absorbs water.

facts.text: The digestive tract is one continuous tube of hollow organs: the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and anus.
Because the mouth and anus both open to the outside, food inside the digestive tract is technically outside the body until it is absorbed.

The liver, pancreas and gallbladder are digestive organs outside the tube that add digestive juices; the small intestine absorbs most nutrients, and the large intestine (which includes the colon) absorbs water and turns waste into stool.

title: Peristalsis moves food
description: Waves of muscle contraction, peristalsis, push food along the tract, so swallowing does not depend on gravity, even upside down or in orbit.

facts.text: Food moves through the digestive tract by peristalsis, waves of muscle contraction that push it along; it does not depend on gravity, and swallowed food can travel the esophagus even upside down.
On February 20, 1962, aboard Friendship 7, astronaut John Glenn ate applesauce from a tube while weightless in orbit.

title: The kinds of teeth
description: Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars crush and grind; children have 20 primary teeth and adults 32 permanent ones, and digestion starts with chewing and saliva.

facts.text: Incisors have narrow edges for cutting into food, canines tear it, and premolars and molars crush and grind it; molars do most of the chewing.
Most children have 20 primary teeth, and most adults have 32 permanent teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars.
Digestion starts in the mouth: chewing breaks food into pieces, and saliva moistens it and contains an enzyme that starts breaking down starches.

title: Tooth enamel
description: Enamel is the hardest substance in the body, about 95 percent mineral, mostly calcium phosphate; it holds no living cells once formed, so it cannot regrow.

facts.text: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body; by weight it is about 95 percent mineral, mostly crystals of calcium phosphate.
Once formed, enamel contains no living cells, because the cells that made it are lost when the tooth erupts; unlike bone, enamel cannot remodel or regrow.

title: How the stomach digests
description: Stomach glands release hydrochloric acid and pepsin, muscles churn food into chyme, and a bicarbonate-rich mucus coat plus a lining renewed every few days keep the stomach from digesting itself.

facts.text: Glands in the stomach lining release hydrochloric acid, which makes stomach contents strongly acidic, kills many swallowed bacteria and turns pepsinogen into pepsin, an enzyme that breaks down proteins.
Stomach muscles mix food with gastric juice until it becomes a thick liquid called chyme, which passes into the small intestine.
The stomach is protected from digesting itself by a thick coat of bicarbonate-rich mucus that neutralizes acid, and its surface lining is replaced every few days.

title: Beaumont's window into the stomach
description: After an 1822 gunshot left Alexis St. Martin with a permanent opening into his stomach, William Beaumont studied digestion through it, publishing in 1833 that acidic gastric juice dissolves food.

facts.text: Before the 1800s, many physicians thought the stomach cooked food with internal heat; others thought digestion was fermentation or putrefaction.

In 1822, Alexis St. Martin, a 19-year-old fur trapper, was shot at close range at a trading post in what is now Michigan; army surgeon William Beaumont treated him, and the wound healed with a permanent opening into his stomach.
Beaumont lowered foods on a silk string through the opening to time their digestion and drew out gastric juice; his 1833 book reported that the juice contained hydrochloric acid and dissolved food.
St. Martin reported pain and distress during some experiments and at one point left for Canada without Beaumont's consent.

title: How the intestines absorb
description: The small intestine does most digestion and absorbs almost all nutrients through villi and microvilli; nutrients go in the blood to the liver first; the large intestine absorbs water, and its bacteria make vitamin K.

facts.text: The small intestine is where most digestion happens and almost all nutrients are absorbed.

The small intestine's lining is covered in tiny finger-like projections called villi, and the cells on the villi carry even tinier projections called microvilli; together they greatly enlarge the surface that absorbs nutrients.
Absorbed simple sugars, amino acids, glycerol and some vitamins and salts travel in the blood to the liver first, while the lymphatic system carries fatty acids and some vitamins.
In the large intestine, water is absorbed, and bacteria help break down remaining nutrients and make vitamin K.

title: The gut's real surface area
description: Textbooks long said the gut's inner surface rivals a tennis court; a 2014 measurement found about 30 to 40 square meters, half a badminton court, mostly in the small intestine.

facts.text: Older textbooks and reference works put the inner surface of the digestive tract at about 180 to 300 square meters, as big as a tennis court or bigger.
In 2014, Herbert Helander and Lars Fändriks used microscope measurements to find the digestive tract's inner surface is about 30 to 40 square meters in healthy adults, about half a badminton court.
Most of the digestive tract's inner surface is in the small intestine; the large intestine adds only about 2 square meters.

title: The liver's many jobs
description: The liver, the body's largest gland, gets nutrient-rich blood from the gut first; it makes bile for fats, stores glycogen and vitamins, breaks down old red blood cells and clears wastes.

facts.text: The liver is the largest gland in the body, weighing about 1.2 to 1.6 kg in adults.
The liver stores, processes and delivers nutrients to the rest of the body when they are needed.
The liver makes bile, which helps digest fats; the gallbladder stores bile between meals and squeezes it into the small intestine when you eat.
The liver also stores glycogen and some vitamins, breaks down old red blood cells and removes wastes and harmful substances from the blood.

title: The liver grows back
description: Up to two-thirds of a healthy liver can be removed and the remaining cells multiply until it is back to about its original size, over weeks to months.

facts.text: In Greek myth, Zeus sent an eagle to eat Prometheus's liver, which kept growing back.
Up to two-thirds of a healthy liver can be surgically removed; the remaining liver cells divide and enlarge until the organ is back to about its original size, over weeks to months in people.

title: Kidneys and nephrons
description: Two fist-sized kidneys below the rib cage hold about a million nephrons each; a glomerulus filters the blood and a tubule returns what the body needs.

facts.text: The kidneys are two bean-shaped organs, each about the size of a fist, just below the rib cage on either side of the spine.
Each kidney holds about a million filtering units called nephrons.
In each nephron, a filter called the glomerulus lets water, wastes and other small molecules through while holding back blood cells and proteins, and a tubule returns needed substances to the blood.

title: How much the kidneys filter
description: The kidneys filter about 150 to 180 liters of fluid a day and return about 99 percent to the blood, leaving about 1 to 2 liters of urine.

facts.text: The kidneys filter about 150 to 180 liters of fluid from the blood each day; about 99 percent is returned to the blood, leaving about 1 to 2 liters of urine.

title: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats
description: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are the three main nutrients; digestion breaks them into simple sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids and glycerol, and glucose is cells' main fuel.

facts.text: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are the three main nutrients in foods and drinks.
Digestion breaks carbohydrates into simple sugars, proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
Carbohydrates such as sugars and starches are turned by the body into glucose, the main source of energy for its cells, tissues and organs.
Fats give the body energy, about twice as many calories per gram as protein or carbohydrate, and help it absorb vitamins.
Proteins are chains of amino acids; the body can make some amino acids, but the essential ones must come from food.

title: Vitamins and minerals
description: Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients, needed in very small amounts but critical for health; there are 13 essential vitamins, and minerals such as calcium and phosphorus keep bones, muscles, heart and brain working.

facts.text: Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients: the body needs them in very small amounts, but they are critical for health.
There are 13 essential vitamins, substances the body needs for normal cell function, growth and development.
The body uses minerals, such as calcium and phosphorus, for jobs including keeping bones, muscles, heart and brain working properly.

title: What a calorie is
description: A calorie is a unit of energy, the heat that warms 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius; the food Calorie is a kilocalorie; food energy is released in digestion and used by cells.

facts.text: A calorie is a unit of energy: the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius.
The Calorie on food labels is a kilocalorie, equal to 1,000 small calories.
Food supplies energy that is released when it is broken down, and cells use that energy for their functions, including building proteins.

title: Measuring the energy in food and people
description: From 1896, Wilbur Atwater's respiration calorimeter showed energy is conserved in the human body and gave the 4, 9 and 4 Calories per gram used for food energy today.

facts.text: From 1896, Wilbur Atwater's team at Wesleyan University ran about 500 experiments in a respiration calorimeter, a small sealed room where volunteers stayed, sometimes for days, while their heat and carbon dioxide output were measured.
Atwater's calorimeter showed that the law of conservation of energy holds for the human body and made it possible to calculate the energy values of foods.
Atwater's system estimates about 4 Calories per gram of protein or carbohydrate and about 9 per gram of fat, and it is still used to calculate the energy in foods.

title: Bodies need different amounts of energy
description: How much energy a body uses varies with age, sex, body size, activity and metabolic rate; the brain, about 2 percent of body weight, uses about 20 percent of the body's calories.

facts.text: How much energy a person needs varies with age, sex, body size, physical activity and metabolic rate.
The brain is about 2 percent of an adult's body weight but uses about 20 percent of the body's oxygen and calories, at a fairly constant rate whatever you are doing.

title: Vitamin C and scurvy
description: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen; humans cannot make it; without it connective tissue weakens into scurvy, with bleeding gums, loose teeth and poor healing.

facts.text: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, a structural protein in skin, blood vessels, bones, cartilage and other connective tissues.
Many animals make their own vitamin C, but humans, other primates, guinea pigs and some bats cannot, because they lack a working enzyme needed to make it.

Without enough vitamin C, collagen isn't made properly and connective tissue weakens: scurvy brings tiredness, joint pain, swollen and bleeding gums, loose teeth and poor wound healing, can appear within about a month, and can be fatal untreated.

title: James Lind's scurvy trial
description: In 1747 James Lind compared six remedies in 12 sailors and saw citrus work best, but he blamed scurvy mainly on damp air and poor digestion, recommended boiled rob, and the Navy adopted lemon juice only in 1795.

facts.text: In May 1747 aboard HMS Salisbury, naval surgeon James Lind gave 12 sailors with scurvy six remedies then in use, two men per remedy: cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, seawater, oranges and lemons, and a medicinal paste.
The two sailors given oranges and lemons improved fastest; one was fit for duty within about six days.
Lind's comparison is regarded as an early example of a controlled clinical trial.
Lind did not see scurvy as a deficiency disease: he blamed it mainly on damp air and a coarse diet the body failed to digest, and his 1753 Treatise did not clearly declare citrus the cure.
Lind later recommended rob, a juice concentrate made by heating fruit juice for hours, but heat destroys vitamin C.
The Royal Navy made lemon juice a standard issue for sailors in 1795, 48 years after Lind's trial, after Gilbert Blane persuaded the Admiralty.
Vitamin C was first isolated in 1928 by Albert Szent-Györgyi and identified in 1932 as the factor that prevents scurvy.

title: From food to a cell's energy
description: Digested sugars are absorbed into the blood, pass the liver, and are carried to cells, where mitochondria combine food molecules with oxygen to release their energy; spare fuel is stored.

facts.text: The circulatory system carries absorbed nutrients to the rest of the body, where they are used for energy, growth and cell repair or stored.
The body can use fuel from food right away or store its energy in tissues such as the liver, muscles and body fat.
In cellular respiration, cells combine oxygen with food molecules to release their chemical energy; in human cells the steps take place in the mitochondria.

title: Central and peripheral nervous system
description: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system; the nerves that reach everywhere else form the peripheral nervous system, carrying signals both ways.

facts.text: The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system (PNS) is everything else, such as the nerves. The brain sits inside the skull and the spinal cord inside the backbone.
Sensory neurons carry information from the sense organs to the brain, and motor neurons carry messages from the brain to the muscles, running down the spinal cord and out along nerves.

title: Voluntary and automatic control
description: The somatic nervous system runs voluntary responses such as moving skeletal muscles; the autonomic nervous system runs involuntary ones such as heart muscle, smooth muscle and glands.

facts.text: Voluntary responses (contracting skeletal muscle) are governed by the somatic nervous system; involuntary responses (smooth muscle, heart muscle, glands such as sweat glands) are governed by the autonomic nervous system.

title: How many neurons
description: A 2009 count by Azevedo and colleagues found about 86 billion neurons in the adult human brain, replacing an unsupported round figure of 100 billion.

facts.text: Frederico Azevedo and colleagues (2009) counted on average about 86 billion neurons in adult male human brains (four brains), plus about 85 billion other, non-neuronal cells.
To count neurons, the 2009 team dissolved brain tissue into an even soup of free cell nuclei, stained and counted the nuclei in samples, and scaled up.
Before 2009, textbooks gave about 100 billion neurons, a round number with no published peer-reviewed count behind it.

title: The parts of a neuron
description: A neuron has dendrites that receive messages, a cell body holding the nucleus, and an axon that sends messages on; information flows one way through it.

facts.text: A neuron has three parts: branch-like dendrites that receive messages, a cell body containing the nucleus, and a tail-like axon that sends messages on to another neuron, a muscle or other cells.
Information flows through a neuron in one direction: from the dendrites, across the cell body, and down the axon.
Some axons are very short, reaching a cell less than a hair's width away; others are very long, carrying messages from the brain all the way down the spinal cord.

title: How a neuron sends a signal
description: A signal travels along the axon as electricity, sped up by insulating myelin, then crosses the synapse as chemical neurotransmitters that attach to the next cell.

facts.text: Neurons use electrical and chemical signals: a signal travels along the axon electrically, and at its end tiny sacs release neurotransmitters that cross a tiny gap, the synapse, and attach to receptors on the next cell.
Myelin, a fatty insulating sheath wrapped around many axons, helps nerve signals travel faster and farther.

title: The reflex arc
description: In a withdrawal reflex, a signal runs from skin sensors to the spinal cord and straight out to a motor neuron, so the body acts before the brain registers pain.

facts.text: When you touch a hot stove, you pull your hand away, typically before you have even registered the pain.
In the withdrawal reflex, skin sensors detect the heat, a signal travels along a sensory fiber to the spinal cord, connects there to a motor neuron, and the biceps contracts to pull the hand away.
Simple reflexes do not include the higher brain centers used for conscious, voluntary movement; the spinal cord handles them.
During the withdrawal, the spinal cord also stops the opposing triceps from contracting, which makes the withdrawal faster.

title: The stretch reflex
description: When a muscle is stretched, a sensor in it triggers the muscle to contract, keeping it at a steady length; the knee jerk is the classic example.

facts.text: In the stretch reflex, a stretched muscle's sensor makes that muscle contract, helping keep muscles at a constant length; the knee jerk from a rubber hammer on the tendon below the kneecap is the classic example.
In the stretch reflex the sensory neuron connects directly to the motor neuron, making it very fast; it is why your head jerks back up when you nod off sitting up.

title: The main parts of the brain
description: The brainstem runs vital functions, the cerebellum coordinates movement, and the cerebrum, the largest part, handles conscious thought; the cerebellum holds most of the neurons.

facts.text: The brain works like a group of experts: all its parts work together, but each has its own special responsibilities.

The brainstem links the brain to the spinal cord and controls vital functions such as breathing and heart rate; the cerebellum coordinates movement, including learned movements like playing piano; the cerebrum, the largest part, is the source of conscious thought, memory and planning.
The cerebral cortex is about 82 percent of the brain's mass but holds about 16 billion neurons (19 percent); the cerebellum, about 10 percent of the mass, holds about 69 billion, roughly 80 percent.

title: The four lobes
description: Each cerebral hemisphere has frontal, parietal, occipital and temporal lobes, each specializing in different work, from planning to vision to hearing and memory.

facts.text: The frontal lobes, behind the forehead, handle planning and voluntary movement; the parietal lobes take in touch and temperature; the occipital lobes at the back process images from the eyes; the temporal lobes handle hearing and help form memories.
Damage to the occipital lobes can cause blindness.

title: Two hemispheres
description: The cerebrum has two hemispheres linked by the corpus callosum; each controls the opposite side of the body, and some jobs, like forming words, lean to one side.

facts.text: A deep groove splits the cerebrum into two halves, the hemispheres, which communicate through a thick bundle of nerve fibers called the corpus callosum.
Signals cross over, so the right hemisphere mainly controls the left side of the body and the left hemisphere the right; a stroke in the right hemisphere can paralyze the left arm and leg.
Some jobs lean to one side: for most people, forming words and speech rely mainly on the left hemisphere, while the right leads in spatial tasks and attention.

title: The left-brained, right-brained myth
description: The popular idea that logical people are left-brained and creative people right-brained is not supported: a 2013 study of 1,011 brain scans found no one with a stronger side overall.

facts.text: A popular idea says logical, detail-oriented people are left-brained and creative, subjective people are right-brained.

In 2013, Jared Nielsen, Jeff Anderson and colleagues at the University of Utah analyzed resting brain scans of 1,011 people aged 7 to 29, split into about 7,000 regions, and found no one with a stronger left or right network overall.
The study found that lateralization is a property of particular connections and regions, such as language areas, not of a whole person's brain.

title: The hippocampus and new memories
description: The case of Henry Molaison showed that the hippocampus is needed to turn new experiences into lasting memories, while skills rely on other systems.

facts.text: In 1953, surgeons removed tissue from each side of 27-year-old Henry Molaison's brain, including much of his hippocampus, to control severe seizures; afterward he could not form new long-term memories.
Molaison kept memories from before the surgery, such as scenes from his childhood, but minutes after meeting someone he had no recollection of the meeting.
The hippocampus, deep inside the brain, acts as a memory indexer, sending memories to the right part of the cerebrum for long-term storage and retrieving them when needed.
Molaison got better at tracing patterns while watching his hand in a mirror, though he could never recall doing the task, showing that skills rely on different memory systems.

title: Forgetting and spacing
description: Ebbinghaus showed that most forgetting happens soon after learning; spacing study out over time makes memories last longer than cramming.

facts.text: Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory with nonsense syllables and in 1885 described the forgetting curve: forgetting is fastest soon after learning, then slows.
Long-term memory is better when learning is spaced out over time rather than crammed into one session, one of the most replicated findings in psychology.

title: The stages of sleep
description: Sleep cycles through three non-REM stages, from light to deep, and REM sleep, when the eyes dart, the brain is nearly as active as awake and the limbs are paralyzed.

facts.text: You spend about one third of your time asleep, and your brain and body stay remarkably active while you sleep.

Non-REM has three stages: stage 1, a changeover of several minutes as heartbeat and breathing slow and muscles twitch; stage 2, light sleep as body temperature drops and eye movements stop; stage 3, deep sleep with the slowest brain waves, when you may be hard to wake.

REM sleep first occurs about 90 minutes after falling asleep: the eyes move rapidly, brain waves become close to waking, and arm and leg muscles are temporarily paralyzed, which stops you acting out dreams.
You cycle through non-REM and REM sleep several times a night; deep stage 3 sleep comes in longer periods in the first half of the night, and REM periods grow longer later on.

title: Why we sleep
description: Sleep's exact purpose is still a mystery; it likely helps consolidate memories, and the idea that it flushes toxins from the brain is actively debated.

facts.text: Everyone needs sleep, but its biological purpose remains a mystery; memory consolidation most likely requires both non-REM and REM sleep.
A 2013 NIH-funded study in mice, led by Maiken Nedergaard, suggested the space between brain cells grows during sleep, letting fluid flush out toxins that build up while awake.
In 2024, a mouse study by Nicholas Franks, William Wisden and colleagues found brain clearance was reduced, not increased, during sleep, and scientists are still debating the idea.

title: Dreams and REM sleep
description: Rapid eye movements in sleep were discovered in the early 1950s and linked to dreaming; everyone dreams, most vividly in REM, though dreams occur in other stages too.

facts.text: In December 1951, Eugene Aserinsky taped electrodes to the head of his 8-year-old son, Armond, before bed; hours later the recording pens swung as if the boy were awake and looking around, but he was fast asleep.
In 1953, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman of the University of Chicago reported regular periods of rapid eye movements during sleep; sleepers woken during them were dreaming, often vividly.
Everyone dreams, for about two hours a night, though most dreams are not remembered; dreams can happen in all sleep stages but are usually most vivid in REM sleep.

title: Theories of dreaming
description: Why we dream is not known. Leading ideas include Freud's disguised wishes, the activation-synthesis hypothesis, and dreams helping process emotions and memories.

facts.text: In The Interpretation of Dreams (1899), Sigmund Freud argued that dreams are disguised wish fulfillments.
In 1977, J. Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley proposed the activation-synthesis hypothesis: during REM sleep the brainstem fires off signals, and the forebrain builds a story to make sense of them.
The exact purpose of dreaming is not known; some scientists think dreams may help process emotions or sort memories.

title: Adrenaline and fight or flight
description: In danger, nerves from the hypothalamus trigger the adrenal glands to release adrenaline within seconds, raising heart rate and blood sugar and preparing the body to fight or flee.

facts.text: The hypothalamus, deep in the brain, gets the adrenaline flowing during a test or a job interview.
In danger or stress, a nerve pathway from the hypothalamus triggers the adrenal glands to release epinephrine (adrenaline) into the blood within seconds.

Adrenaline raises heart rate and blood pressure, widens the airways, releases glucose into the blood, diverts blood from the gut and skin to muscles and brain, widens the pupils, and can bring a dry mouth and lost appetite.
The American physiologist Walter Cannon described the fight-or-flight response in the early 1900s and coined the phrase.

title: Nerve signals and hormones
description: Nerves send fast, local chemical messages; hormones travel through the blood to distant targets and usually act more slowly; in an emergency the two work together.

facts.text: Neurotransmitters act locally and quickly: the target cell responds within milliseconds, and the response stops soon after the signal ends.
Hormones are released by glands and carried mainly by the bloodstream throughout the body to target cells, so they usually act more slowly than nerves; some take up to 48 hours.
Fight-or-flight hormones act fast because the two systems are connected: the quick nervous system is what stimulates the adrenal glands to release them.

title: Sense, decide, act
description: The nervous system has three basic jobs: sensation (taking in information), integration (weighing it against memories and circumstances) and response.

facts.text: The nervous system's basic functions are sensation, integration and response; in integration, input is weighed against other input, memories and your state before a response is chosen.
A batter seeing a pitch does not swing automatically: the ball's speed and path, and the game situation, are weighed before deciding to swing or let it pass.

title: The brain's energy budget
description: The brain is about 2 percent of body weight but uses about 20 percent of the body's energy at rest, and hard thinking adds very little.

facts.text: The adult brain is about 2 percent of body weight but uses about 20 percent of the oxygen and calories the body consumes at rest.
The brain's energy use stays remarkably constant; a hard mental task adds only a tiny amount on top of its large baseline.

title: Senses beyond the classic five
description: Aristotle listed five senses, but the body also senses balance, body position and movement, temperature, pain and inner states like hunger.

facts.text: Aristotle listed five senses (sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell) in his work De Anima (On the Soul) and argued there is no sixth.
