Proprioceptors in muscles, tendons and joints keep a continuous report on the position and movement of the limbs, so you can sense where they are without looking.
Beyond the classic five, the body senses balance (through organs in the inner ear), temperature and pain, and receptors in the digestive tract help create hunger and thirst.

title: How many senses? It depends how you count
description: There is no agreed number of human senses: proposals range from six or seven to between 22 and 33, depending on how a separate sense is defined.

facts.text: In 2024, neurologists Thomas Brandt, Marianne Dieterich and Doreen Huppert proposed recognizing balance and body position sense as a sixth and seventh sense.
Philosopher Barry Smith reports that neuroscientist Charles Spence's colleagues put the number of human senses anywhere between 22 and 33.
There is no agreed number of human senses; the count depends on how a separate sense is defined, and researchers classify senses inconsistently.

title: How the eye focuses light
description: The cornea bends incoming light, the iris sets the size of the pupil, and the lens works with the cornea to focus light onto the retina.

facts.text: Light enters the eye through the cornea, the clear dome-shaped front layer, which bends it; the colored iris controls how much light passes through the pupil.
The lens works together with the cornea to focus light onto the retina, a light-sensitive layer of tissue at the back of the eye.

title: From retina to brain
description: Photoreceptors turn light into electrical signals that the optic nerve carries to the brain, which builds the image, turns the inverted retinal image upright and fills in the blind spot.

facts.text: Photoreceptor cells in the retina turn light into electrical signals, which travel through the optic nerve to the brain, and the brain turns them into the images you see.
The cornea and lens together act like a convex lens, so the image formed on the retina is upside down; the brain corrects for this, and we see the world upright.
Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina, a patch with no rods or cones; we rarely notice it because the two eyes' views overlap and the brain fills in or ignores the gap.

title: Cones and color
description: Rods work in dim light; cones work in bright light and give color. Three types of cone each respond best to different wavelengths, and the brain combines them.

facts.text: The retina has two kinds of light-sensing cell: rods, which provide vision in low light, and cones, which provide vision in bright light, including color vision.
There are three types of cone, each with a pigment most sensitive to particular wavelengths of light, and the brain combines input from all three to produce color vision.

title: Color blindness
description: Red-green color blindness, the most common kind, affects about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women of Northern European ancestry, because its genes sit on the X chromosome; John Dalton first described it.

facts.text: The most common type of color vision deficiency makes it hard to tell the difference between red and green.
Among people with Northern European ancestry, red-green color blindness affects about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women.
The genes for red-green color blindness are passed down on the X chromosome; males have one X chromosome, so one copy is enough, while females must have the gene on both X chromosomes.
In 1794 the chemist John Dalton described his own and his brother's color vision to the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society, the first published account of color blindness.
Dalton guessed that the jelly-like fluid in his eyes was tinted blue and asked for his eyes to be examined after his death; in 1844 the fluid was found to be colorless.
In 1995, DNA from Dalton's preserved eye showed he lacked the gene for the medium-wavelength (green-sensitive) cone pigment.

title: Nearsightedness and farsightedness
description: When the eye's shape keeps light from focusing on the retina, nearsighted eyes focus it in front (far things blur) and farsighted eyes focus it behind (near things blur).

facts.text: Refractive errors happen when the shape of the eye keeps light from focusing correctly on the retina, for example when the eyeball is too long or too short or the cornea is misshaped.
In nearsightedness (myopia), light focuses in front of the retina instead of on it, often because the eyeball is too long, so far-away objects look blurry.
In farsightedness (hyperopia), light focuses behind the retina instead of on it, often because the eyeball is too short, so nearby objects look blurry.

title: How glasses and contacts fix focus
description: Concave lenses spread light so the focus moves back onto the retina (nearsightedness); convex lenses bring it together (farsightedness). Contacts do the same on the eye's surface.

facts.text: A concave lens, thinner in the middle, spreads light rays apart and corrects nearsightedness; a convex lens, thicker in the middle, brings rays together and corrects farsightedness.
A contact lens is a thin artificial lens worn on the surface of the eye to correct refractive errors, as a substitute for eyeglasses.
The earliest eyeglasses, which in Europe first appeared in Italy, had convex lenses to help farsighted people.
Raphael's portrait of Pope Leo X, painted in the late 1510s (dated 1517 to about 1519), shows the nearsighted pope holding a concave lens, an early picture of a lens for myopia.

title: The path of sound through the ear
description: Sound vibrates the eardrum; three tiny middle-ear bones (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify the vibrations and pass them to the fluid-filled cochlea.

facts.text: Hearing turns sound waves in the air into electrical signals, which the auditory nerve carries to the brain.
Sound waves travel down the ear canal to the eardrum, which vibrates and passes the vibrations to three tiny middle-ear bones, the malleus, incus and stapes, which amplify them.
The stapes, or stirrup, is the smallest of the three middle-ear bones and is shaped like a stirrup.
The middle-ear bones pass the vibrations to the cochlea, a snail-shaped, fluid-filled structure in the inner ear.

title: Hair cells in the cochlea
description: In the cochlea, hair cells ride a traveling wave, sorted by pitch; bending their bristles creates electrical signals. Human hair cells do not grow back.

facts.text: In the cochlea, vibrations set off a traveling wave on the basilar membrane; hair cells near the wide end detect high-pitched sounds, and those near the center detect low-pitched sounds.
As hair cells move, tiny bristles on top (stereocilia) bend, opening channels that let chemicals rush in and create an electrical signal.
Unlike the hair cells of birds and amphibians, human hair cells don't grow back; most noise-induced hearing loss is caused by their damage and death.

title: The inner ear's balance organs
description: The vestibular system has three fluid-filled semicircular canals that sense head rotation and two pouches, the utricle and saccule, whose tiny grains sense gravity.

facts.text: The part of the inner ear that handles balance is the vestibular system, or labyrinth, a maze-like structure of bone and soft tissue that sits beside the cochlea.
Three fluid-filled semicircular canals, looped at roughly right angles to one another, sense head rotation: when the head turns, the fluid moves and bends hair cells, signaling which way it turned.
In the utricle and saccule, hair cells sit under a gel holding tiny grains of calcium carbonate; gravity pulls on the grains, telling the brain whether the head is upright, tilted back or lying down.

title: When balance signals disagree
description: The brain builds balance from the eyes, inner ears and body sensors; when they disagree (after spinning, or below deck on a ship) you feel dizzy or motion sick.

facts.text: The sense of balance relies on signals to the brain from the eyes, the inner ears, and the muscles and touch sensors in the legs.
After you spin and stop, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving, so the inner ear signals motion while the eyes show you are still, and you feel dizzy.
The most widely accepted explanation of motion sickness is sensory conflict: in a ship cabin with no outside view, the inner ear reports motion while the eyes suggest you are not moving.

title: Taste buds and the five basic tastes
description: Taste cells in taste buds on the tongue, palate and throat detect at least five basic tastes (sweet, sour, bitter, salty, umami), and every taste area senses all of them: the tongue map is a myth.

facts.text: Taste cells are clustered in taste buds on the tongue and the roof of the mouth and along the lining of the throat.
Taste cells respond to at least five basic tastes: sweet, sour, bitter, salty and umami, the savory taste of glutamate, found in foods such as broth, meat extracts and some cheeses.
The tongue map is a misconception: taste cells for different tastes are scattered across the tongue, and every area with taste buds senses all the basic tastes.
The tongue map grew out of a 1901 study by David Hanig that found only tiny differences in taste sensitivity around the tongue, redrawn in the 1940s by Harvard psychologist Edwin Boring.

title: Flavor is mostly smell
description: Smell cells high in the nose get aromas through the nostrils and, while you chew, from the back of the throat; flavor blends these smells with taste, temperature and texture.

facts.text: Smell comes from olfactory sensory neurons in a small patch of tissue high inside the nose; odors reach them through the nostrils and, as you chew, through a channel from the roof of the throat to the nose.
Flavor combines the basic tastes with sensations of heat, cold and texture and a food's aroma; it is flavor that tells a pear from an apple, and when a cold blocks the nose, food tastes bland.

title: The skin's sensors, and why pain matters
description: Skin sensors come in families for touch, temperature, pain and chemicals, crowded most densely in fingertips and lips; pain is a warning signal, as people born without it show.

facts.text: Somatosensory receptors fall into four categories: mechanoreceptors (touch and pressure), thermoreceptors (temperature), nociceptors (pain) and chemoreceptors.
Free nerve endings are the most common nerve endings in the skin and respond to painful stimuli, to hot and cold, and to light touch.
Touch receptors are denser in hairless skin such as the fingertips and lips, which is more sensitive, and less dense in hairy skin such as the arms, legs and torso.

Pain is a vital signal that helps people avoid danger; people born unable to feel pain can still tell hot from cold but not that a drink is burning their tongue, have more injuries and may live shorter lives.
Channelopathy-associated congenital insensitivity to pain is a rare condition caused by variants in a single gene, SCN9A.

title: Sensors for heat, cold and touch
description: David Julius used chili pepper capsaicin to find TRPV1, a sensor for painful heat; he and Ardem Patapoutian used menthol to find the cold sensor TRPM8, and Patapoutian found the touch sensor Piezo2 (2021 Nobel Prize).

facts.text: David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering receptors for temperature and touch.

In the late 1990s, Julius used capsaicin, the chili pepper compound that causes a burning feeling, to find TRPV1, a sensor in nerve endings that is switched on by heat at temperatures felt as painful.
Julius and Patapoutian each independently used menthol to identify TRPM8, a sensor switched on by cold.
Patapoutian discovered Piezo2, a pressure sensor that is essential for the sense of touch and plays a key role in sensing body position and movement.

title: Optical illusions
description: An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts reality, often because of how the brain interprets what the eyes send; the Muller-Lyer lines are a classic example.

facts.text: An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts objective reality; illusions can come from light or poor lighting, from the eye itself, and from how the brain processes visual information.

In the Muller-Lyer illusion, published by Franz Carl Muller-Lyer in 1889, two lines of equal length look different: the one with fins flaring outward at its ends looks longer than the one capped with arrowheads.

title: Correcting for shadows
description: The visual system estimates the lighting and judges each surface's own shade despite shadows; Adelson's checker-shadow illusion shows this correction misfiring on a flat picture.

facts.text: In Edward Adelson's 1995 checker-shadow illusion, a square in a cylinder's shadow looks much lighter than a square outside it, although both are exactly the same shade of grey.

The visual system estimates where the light in a scene comes from and judges each surface's own shade regardless of shadow, which keeps objects looking the same color as lighting changes; on a flat picture, that correction misleads.

title: Sensation, transduction and perception
description: Every sense starts with receptors converting a stimulus into a nerve signal (transduction); sensation is that detection, and perception is the brain organizing and interpreting it.

facts.text: Sensory receptors are specialized cells that respond to particular kinds of stimuli, and converting a stimulus's energy into a nerve signal is called transduction.
Sensation is a sensory receptor detecting a stimulus; perception is the way the brain organizes, interprets and consciously experiences that sensory information.

title: Sensory adaptation
description: We often stop perceiving stimuli that stay the same for a long time, which frees attention for change.

facts.text: Sensory adaptation: we often stop perceiving stimuli that stay relatively constant over long periods, such as a light flashing steadily outside a window.

title: Skin, the body's outer wall
description: Skin is the largest organ: an epidermis of epithelial cells over the dermis and hypodermis, topped by dead, keratin-packed cells that block germs and are replaced about every 4 weeks.

facts.text: Skin is the body's largest organ; it covers the whole body and acts as a protective barrier against the outside world.
The skin's primary role is to serve as a physical barrier that protects the body from foreign organisms such as germs.
Skin has three layers: the epidermis of closely packed epithelial cells on top, the dermis with blood vessels, hair follicles and sweat glands, and the mostly fatty hypodermis.
An adult's skin covers about 1.8 square meters.
The outermost layer of the epidermis, the stratum corneum, is made of dry, dead cells filled with keratin that help keep microbes out and stop water loss.
Keratin is a tough fibrous protein that gives hair, nails and skin their hardness and water resistance.
New epidermal cells are made at the base of the epidermis and pushed upward, dying as they go; the outer layer is replaced about every 4 weeks.

title: Skin's chemical and living shields
description: The skin surface is cool, dry and slightly acidic, oil from its glands kills bacteria, and resident microbes crowd out harmful ones.

facts.text: The skin surface is cool, dry and slightly acidic (pH on average below 5), and that acidity holds back harmful bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus.
Oil glands in the skin make an oil that keeps skin from drying out and kills bacteria.
Friendly microbes living on the skin occupy its niches and protect against invasion by more harmful organisms.

title: Three kinds of germ
description: Germs are microbes that cause infectious disease; bacteria are single living cells, most of them harmless, fungi include molds and yeasts, and viruses are not cells at all.

facts.text: Infectious diseases are caused by germs (microbes); the main kinds are bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites.
Bacteria are tiny living things made of a single cell; they multiply quickly and some give off toxins that make you sick.
Most types of bacteria don't make people sick, and some are helpful.
Fungi include mushrooms, molds, mildew and yeasts; they live in air, soil, water and on plants, and some live in the human body.
Athlete's foot is an infection caused by a fungus.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections but do not work against viruses; for most viral infections the immune system does the fighting.

title: Viruses, the hijackers
description: Viruses are genetic material in a protein coat, far smaller than bacteria, and can multiply only by hijacking living cells; they were found in 1892 because they slipped through bacterial filters.

facts.text: A virus is genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat; it is not a cell.
Viruses can multiply only inside living cells: they invade a cell and use it to make copies of themselves.
In 1892, Dmitry Ivanovsky found that a disease of tobacco plants was passed on by an agent small enough to slip through a filter that trapped bacteria.
Most viruses measure from about 20 nanometers to a few hundred nanometers across.

title: Innate immunity and phagocytes
description: Innate immunity is the nonspecific defense you are born with: barriers like skin plus phagocytes, the "devouring cells" Metchnikoff found in starfish larvae in 1882.

facts.text: In 1882, in Messina, Italy, Elie Metchnikoff introduced splinters into see-through starfish larvae and saw certain cells surround and engulf them.
Metchnikoff called the engulfing cells phagocytes, from Greek words meaning "devouring cells," and shared the 1908 Nobel Prize for the discovery.
Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf ("eat") germs and dead or damaged cells.
Innate, or nonspecific, immunity is the defense system you are born with; it includes barriers such as the skin that keep harmful materials out.

title: Acquired immunity: antibodies and memory
description: Acquired immunity develops as you meet germs: B cells make antibodies against a specific antigen, T cells attack directly, and memory cells make the next response faster.

facts.text: Acquired (adaptive) immunity develops with exposure to antigens: the immune system builds a defense against each specific antigen it meets.
Lymphocytes are white blood cells of two types: B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies, and T cells attack antigens directly and help control the immune response.
Antibodies are proteins that attach to one specific antigen, usually a protein on the surface of a germ, and make it easier for immune cells to destroy.
After an infection, some B and T cells remain as memory, so the immune system responds faster and more efficiently the next time it meets the same antigen.

title: Fever: the thermostat turned up
description: In a fever, pyrogens in the blood make the hypothalamus raise the body's temperature set point, so you feel chilly as temperature climbs and warm and sweaty as it falls.

facts.text: The hypothalamus, a part of the brain, regulates body temperature; during a fever it raises the temperature the body aims for.
During an infection, chemicals called pyrogens are carried in the blood to the brain, where they push the hypothalamus's temperature setting up.
While a fever's temperature is rising, a person may feel chilly or even have shaking chills.
When a fever's temperature falls, the person feels warm, and the skin becomes flushed and moist with sweat.

title: Why fever helps
description: Fever's heat stirs white blood cells and antibody production and slows some germs; it is costly but over 600 million years old, and even infected lizards seek warmth.

facts.text: Fever temperatures stimulate white blood cells to move, act and multiply, and increase the production of antibodies.
Higher body temperatures may directly kill or slow the growth of some bacteria and viruses.
Fever is costly: each 1 C rise in body temperature needs a 10 to 12.5 percent increase in metabolic rate.
Fever has been conserved in warm- and cold-blooded vertebrates for over 600 million years.
Desert iguanas are cold-blooded and cannot heat themselves from inside, so when infected they move somewhere warmer; kept from warming by about 2 C, their survival fell by 75 percent.

title: How vaccines train immunity
description: A vaccine imitates an infection with a killed or weakened germ, a part of one or genetic instructions, so the immune system makes antibodies and memory without the disease.

facts.text: Vaccines train the immune system to recognize a germ, make antibodies and remember how to fight it, without causing the illness.
Vaccines work by imitating an infection to engage the body's natural defenses.
A vaccine's antigen can be a killed or weakened form of the germ, a part of it, or genetic instructions (RNA or DNA) that tell your cells to make that part.
After one or more doses, vaccine protection typically lasts years, decades or even a lifetime, and later exposure to the germ is quickly destroyed.

title: Vaccines are safe, effective and shared
description: Vaccines are tested in several trial phases and monitored after use; side effects are usually minor. They protect the unvaccinated around us and have saved at least 154 million lives since 1974.

facts.text: A vaccinated person is far less likely to die or become seriously ill from a disease than someone whose immune system is unprepared.

Vaccines are very safe: each goes through several phases of clinical trials before use and is monitored by health authorities afterward; side effects are usually minor and short, like a sore arm, and serious reactions are extremely rare.
People who cannot be vaccinated, such as very young babies, depend on others being vaccinated to be protected from vaccine-preventable diseases.
A 2024 WHO-led study estimated that immunization saved at least 154 million lives over the past 50 years (since 1974), about 6 every minute, 101 million of them infants.
The 2024 study found immunization to be the single greatest contribution of any health intervention to babies surviving and growing into healthy adults.

title: Variolation before vaccines
description: Before vaccines, people in Africa, India and China deliberately infected healthy people with smallpox material; about 2 to 3 percent died, far fewer than from natural smallpox. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought it to England in 1721.

facts.text: Smallpox killed up to about 3 in 10 (30 percent) of the people who caught it.
In variolation, people who had never had smallpox were exposed to material from smallpox sores, scratched into the arm or breathed in through the nose.
Variolation was practiced in Africa, India and China long before it reached Europe in the 18th century.
About 2 to 3 percent of variolated people died, far fewer than died of smallpox caught naturally.
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who had seen variolation in the Ottoman Empire, had her daughter variolated in London in 1721.

title: Jenner and the first vaccine
description: Milkmaids with cowpox escaped smallpox. In 1796 Jenner inoculated James Phipps with cowpox, then with smallpox, and no disease developed; he named the method vaccination. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.

facts.text: Edward Jenner observed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a disease picked up from cows, did not catch smallpox.
On May 14, 1796, Jenner took material from cowpox sores on the hand of dairymaid Sarah Nelmes and inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps.
In July 1796, Jenner inoculated James Phipps with smallpox matter, and no disease developed.
Jenner was not the first to use cowpox: the farmer Benjamin Jesty had done so earlier, but Jenner tested it and published his results in 1798.
Jenner called his method vaccination, from the Latin vacca, meaning "cow."
In 1980, WHO declared smallpox eradicated, the only human infectious disease ever eradicated; the last natural case was in Somalia in 1977.

title: Fleming's moldy dish
description: In September 1928 Fleming saw Staphylococcus fail to grow near a Penicillium mold that had contaminated a dish left out during his vacation; he named the substance penicillin.

facts.text: In September 1928, Alexander Fleming saw that Staphylococcus bacteria failed to grow near a Penicillium mold that had contaminated a culture dish.
The dish sat on Fleming's bench during a two-week vacation; the mold spore perhaps came through a window, or more likely floated up a stairwell from the lab below.
Fleming realized a substance made by the mold killed the bacteria, and he named it penicillin.
Fleming published his discovery in 1929, but the scientific community took little notice.
Fleming and two young researchers failed to stabilize and purify penicillin, let alone make enough for clinical trials.

title: Florey, Chain and the Oxford team
description: Florey and Chain's Oxford team purified penicillin, grew it even in bedpans, cured infected mice in 1940 and treated a first patient in 1941; a British-American effort mass-produced it and the three men shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.

facts.text: In the late 1930s, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team at Oxford isolated and purified penicillin.
To make enough penicillin, the Oxford team grew the mold in all kinds of vessels, including hospital bedpans.
In a 1940 experiment, four infected mice given penicillin were alive hours later, while four untreated mice were dead.
In February 1941 a policeman became the first patient treated; he improved, then relapsed and died when the supply ran out, despite penicillin recovered from his urine.
Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for penicillin.
At its height, the British-American wartime penicillin effort involved thousands of people and some 35 institutions.
Penicillin works by blocking the enzymes bacteria use to build their cell walls.

title: Semmelweis and childbed fever
description: In 1847 Semmelweis traced higher childbed fever deaths in the students' division to infection carried on hands from the dissecting room; chlorinated lime handwashing cut deaths from about 18 to about 1 percent, but he was rejected.

facts.text: In Ignaz Semmelweis's Vienna maternity clinic, students trained in one division and midwives in the other; childbed fever deaths were two or three times higher in the students' division.
A colleague of Semmelweis died of a wound infection picked up while examining the body of a woman who had died of childbed fever.
Semmelweis reasoned that students coming straight from the dissecting room carried the infection, and in 1847 he ordered them to wash their hands in chlorinated lime solution before each examination.
After handwashing began, deaths in the students' division fell from about 18 percent to about 1 percent.
Most of the medical establishment rejected Semmelweis's teaching; the weight of authority stood against him.

title: Handwashing today
description: The CDC calls soap and water the best way to remove germs in most situations: scrub at least 20 seconds, because friction lifts microbes off skin before hands carry them to your face. It cuts diarrheal illness by 23 to 40 percent.

facts.text: The CDC says washing hands with soap and water is the best way to get rid of germs in most situations, scrubbing for at least 20 seconds (about two runs of "Happy Birthday").
According to the CDC, lathering and scrubbing hands creates friction that helps lift dirt, grease and microbes from skin.
Germs on unwashed hands get into the body when people touch their eyes, nose and mouth.
The CDC reports that handwashing reduces diarrheal illness by 23 to 40 percent and respiratory illnesses such as colds by 16 to 21 percent.

title: How an allergy happens
description: An allergy is the immune system reacting to something harmless: IgE antibodies attach to mast cells, and on a later exposure the mast cells release histamine, which causes symptoms.

facts.text: An allergy is a reaction by the immune system to something that does not bother most other people; in most allergic reactions the immune system is responding to a false alarm.
Common allergens include pollen, dust mites, mold spores, pet dander, foods, insect stings and some medicines.
In an allergy, IgE antibodies against the allergen attach to mast cells, sensitizing them to react the next time that allergen appears.
When the allergen binds to IgE on mast cells, the cells release histamine, which causes symptoms such as a runny nose and swelling.

title: Why some people have allergies
description: Genes and environment both shape allergies, which run in families; about a third of US adults have a diagnosed seasonal allergy, eczema or food allergy, and anaphylaxis can be life-threatening.

facts.text: Genes and environment both play a role in developing allergies; if both parents have allergies, there is a good chance their child will too.
In 2021, 31.8 percent of US adults had a diagnosed seasonal allergy, eczema or food allergy.
Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction that can be life-threatening.

title: Lymph nodes, the immune system's meeting points
description: Lymph nodes sit along the lymph vessels in places like the neck, armpits and groin; with the spleen they are where white blood cells fight infection, which is why infections make them swell.

facts.text: Lymph nodes are glands along the lymph vessels, found in places such as the neck, armpits and groin.
Along with the spleen, lymph nodes are where white blood cells fight infection.
Infections are the most common cause of swollen lymph nodes.

title: Fertilization: egg and sperm make one cell
description: A sperm cell and an egg cell, each carrying 23 chromosomes, fuse into one cell, the zygote, with the full 46: one of each pair from each parent.

facts.text: Development begins at fertilization, when a sperm cell and an egg cell fuse into a single new cell called the zygote.
Each egg or sperm cell carries exactly 23 chromosomes, one of each pair, so the fertilized egg has 46: one of each pair from each parent.

title: From zygote to fetus in about 40 weeks
description: The zygote divides into a ball of cells that specialize into all the body's cell types; the embryo is called a fetus from week 10 of pregnancy, and pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks.

facts.text: In its first days, the zygote divides again and again to form a ball of cells.
As the embryo grows, its cells become more specialized step by step, forming all the cell types of the body, such as nerve, muscle and liver cells.
At the end of week 10 of pregnancy, about 8 weeks after fertilization, the embryo is called a fetus, the stage that lasts until birth.
Pregnancy usually lasts about 40 weeks, counted from the first day of the last menstrual period, which is about two weeks before fertilization.

title: Two versions of each gene, one from each parent
description: You inherit two alleles for each variable stretch of DNA, one from each parent; a dominant allele can mask a recessive one, and random sorting gives each egg or sperm a different mix.

facts.text: For any stretch of DNA that varies between people, you inherit two versions, called alleles: one from each parent.
For a dominant trait, one copy of the dominant allele is enough to show it; the effect of the other, recessive allele is masked.
With 23 chromosome pairs, a person can make over eight million genetically distinct eggs or sperm by random sorting alone, and swapped pieces add more variety.

title: Most traits involve many genes
description: Traits like height and skin color are polygenic and shaped by environment; even eye color involves several genes, not one where brown simply beats blue.

facts.text: Researchers used to think eye color was set by a single gene, with brown eyes dominant over blue.
Eye color depends on how much melanin is in the iris; several genes, led by OCA2 and HERC2, combine to give a continuum of eye colors.
Although it is uncommon, parents with blue eyes can have a child with brown eyes.
A polygenic trait, such as height or skin color, is influenced by two or more genes, and many such traits are also shaped by the environment.

title: Identical and fraternal twins
description: Identical twins come from one fertilized egg that splits and share the same DNA; fraternal twins come from two eggs and two sperm and are as alike as siblings.

facts.text: Identical (monozygotic) twins come from a single egg fertilized by a single sperm; early on, the embryo splits into two.
Identical twins are genetically identical and always the same sex.
Fraternal (dizygotic) twins come from two eggs, each fertilized by a different sperm; they share about half their genes, like other siblings, and can be different sexes.
Identical twins occur in 3 to 4 of every 1,000 births worldwide and mostly don't run in families; fraternal twins are about twice as common and do.
Fraternal twins result when more than one egg is released in a single cycle, which is about twice as likely if a close relative has had fraternal twins.

title: What twins reveal about genes and environment
description: Identical twins have different fingerprints because womb conditions shape fine details; comparing identical and fraternal twins helps separate genes from environment.

facts.text: Even identical twins have different fingerprints: the ridges form from the third to the sixth month of development, and their fine details are shaped by conditions in the womb.

Because identical twins are genetically identical, twin studies help separate the effects of genes and environment; raised apart, identical twins are far more alike than fraternal twins, and their differences reflect the environment.

title: The hormone relay that starts puberty
description: Puberty begins when the hypothalamus releases GnRH, the pituitary releases LH and FSH, and the ovaries or testes release sex hormones; changes typically start between 8 and 14.

facts.text: Puberty is the time of life when sexual maturity takes place; its physical changes typically begin between ages 8 and 13 in girls and 9 and 14 in boys.

Puberty is triggered by the hypothalamus, which releases GnRH; that signals the pituitary to release LH and FSH, which tell the ovaries or testes to release sex hormones such as estrogens and testosterone.
The pituitary is a pea-sized gland connected to the bottom of the hypothalamus.

title: Growth spurts and a brain that matures last
description: The growth spurt peaks around 11.5 in girls and 13.5 in boys, body hair appears, and the brain keeps maturing until the mid-to-late 20s.

facts.text: Girls' growth spurt typically peaks around age 11.5 and slows around 16; boys' peaks around 13.5 and slows around 18.
New body hair usually begins to grow at about age 9 or 10 in girls and about age 12 in boys.
The brain stops growing in size by early adolescence but keeps maturing until the mid-to-late 20s; the prefrontal cortex, used for planning and decisions, is one of the last parts to mature.

title: The Hayflick limit and telomeres
description: Normal human cells divide only about 40 to 60 times (Hayflick, 1961), partly because telomeres at chromosome ends shorten at each division.

facts.text: In 1961 Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead reported that normal human cells grown in a dish divide only about 40 to 60 times before they stop.
Hayflick's finding overturned the claim, made by Alexis Carrel, that cells in culture could keep dividing forever; Hayflick linked the limit to aging.
Each chromosome ends in a telomere of repeated DNA; some repeats are cut off at every division until the telomeres are too short for the cell to divide successfully.

title: Senescent cells and accumulated damage
description: Cells that stop dividing without dying (senescent cells) build up with age and release inflammatory molecules; the WHO describes ageing as accumulated molecular and cellular damage.

facts.text: A cell that stops dividing but does not die is called senescent; senescent cells never divide again and build up in almost all tissues as we age.
Senescent cells release harmful molecules that trigger inflammation and disrupt neighboring cells, like a rotten apple spoiling a barrel, and are linked to many illnesses of aging.
The WHO describes biological ageing as the result of many kinds of molecular and cellular damage building up over time, only loosely tied to age in years.

title: Why life expectancy has risen
description: Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2024 (UN); it was once pulled down by child deaths, and it has risen at all ages thanks to nutrition, sanitation and health care.

facts.text: According to the UN's World Population Prospects 2024, global life expectancy at birth reached 73.3 years in 2024, 8.4 years more than in 1995.
Global life expectancy fell during the COVID-19 pandemic and has been rising again since.
Life expectancy is an average: the number of years a person of a given age can expect to live.

Historically, life expectancy was pulled down by high infant and child mortality: before modern times about a quarter of babies died in their first year and almost half of children before the end of puberty.
Life expectancy has risen at all ages, not only because fewer children die; better nutrition, sanitation, fighting infection and modern health care all contributed.

title: The oldest verified person
description: Jeanne Calment died in 1997 aged 122; a 2018 challenge to her record was rejected by its validators, and most researchers accept it.

facts.text: Jeanne Calment of France, who died in 1997 aged 122 years and 164 days, is the oldest person whose age has been verified.
In 2018 researchers claimed Calment's daughter had taken her identity decades earlier; her age's validators rejected the claim, and most researchers still accept the record.

title: Walking upright, an inheritance millions of years old
description: Walking on two legs goes back to the earliest known humans about 6 million years ago; the shock-absorbing lower-back curve is uniquely human.

facts.text: Walking on two legs is older than our species: the oldest evidence for it comes from fossils of the earliest known humans, about 6 million years ago.
The curve of your lower back, which absorbs shock when you walk, is uniquely human; a similar curve appears in the spine of the early human Australopithecus africanus.

title: A big brain and a young species
description: Brain size tripled over human evolution; Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago and is one of more than 200 primate species.

facts.text: The earliest humans had brains about the size of a chimpanzee's; over human evolution brain size tripled, growing fastest during a time of dramatic climate change.
Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago.
Fossils and DNA confirm that humans are one of more than 200 species of primates, and Neanderthals are our closest extinct relatives.

title: Neanderthal DNA in living people
description: Our species interbred with Neanderthals; about 1 to 4 percent of the DNA of people of European or Asian descent is Neanderthal (Pääbo, Nobel 2022).

facts.text: Svante Pääbo's team published the first Neanderthal genome in 2010 and showed our species interbred with Neanderthals; about 1 to 4 percent of the DNA of people of European or Asian descent comes from them.
Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the genomes of extinct human relatives.

title: Vestigial traits: goosebumps and the tailbone
description: Vestigial structures are leftovers from ancestors with little apparent function, like the goosebump muscle and the embryo's lost tail, though some still do jobs.

facts.text: Biologists call structures vestigial when they have little or no apparent function and appear to be residual parts from a past common ancestor; they are one line of evidence for evolution.
Wings on flightless birds and hind leg bones in whales are classic examples of vestigial structures.
Each hair has a small muscle, the arrector pili, that can make it stand up; on a furry animal such as a frightened cat this traps insulating air, and on humans it shows as goose bumps.
In 2020, Harvard researchers found in mice that the muscle and nerve behind goosebumps also help regulate the stem cells that grow new hair.
Human embryos, like those of other great apes, have a tail that is lost before birth.
The tailbone, or coccyx, is a remnant of a tail, yet it anchors muscles, supports tendons and ligaments, and helps bear your weight when you sit, like one leg of a tripod.

title: The appendix: vestigial but not useless
description: The appendix has immune tissue and may shelter helpful gut bacteria; it evolved independently over 30 times in mammals.

facts.text: The appendix, a small tube attached to the start of the large intestine, has immune tissue and may shelter helpful gut bacteria that restock the gut after an illness.
A 2017 study of 533 mammal species found the appendix evolved independently over 30 times and almost never disappears from a lineage once it appears.

title: Circadian rhythms and the master clock
description: Body rhythms follow a roughly 24-hour cycle set mainly by light and run by the SCN master clock, which controls melatonin; in teens melatonin timing runs later.

facts.text: Circadian rhythms are the physical, mental and behavioral changes the body goes through over a 24-hour cycle, and light and dark influence them most.
Nearly every tissue and organ has its own circadian rhythm, and these rhythms shape sleep patterns, hormone release, appetite and digestion, and body temperature.

The body's master clock is a group of nerve cells in the brain called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN); it controls melatonin based on the light the eyes receive, making more in the evening, which causes sleepiness.
Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young won the 2017 Nobel Prize for uncovering how the body clock works, studying fruit flies.
In teens, melatonin stays high later at night and drops later in the morning than in children and adults, which may explain why many teens stay up late and struggle to wake early.

title: Why jet lag happens
description: Crossing time zones leaves the body clock on home time; it adapts about 1 hour a day eastward and 1.5 westward, because the inner clock runs slightly long.

facts.text: Jet lag is a temporary mismatch between the body clock and local time after fast travel across time zones; for the first days, rhythms stay anchored to the departure time zone.
The body clock adapts about 1 hour a day after eastward flights and about 1.5 hours a day after westward ones; west is easier because the inner clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours.
Light helps set the body clock to the local day, and it can shorten how long jet lag lasts.

title: Epigenetics: switches on the DNA
description: Chemical tags such as methyl groups switch genes on or off without changing the DNA letters; identical twins' tags drift apart with age.

facts.text: Epigenetics is how cells turn genes on or off with chemical tags attached to DNA, without changing the DNA sequence itself.
A common tag is a methyl group; when methyl groups sit on a gene, that gene is turned off.
Diet and pollutants can change epigenetic tags, and cells keep the tags as they divide.
A 2005 study found identical twins have nearly indistinguishable epigenetic tags when young, while older identical twins differ markedly.

title: WHO's healthy-diet principles
description: WHO describes a healthy diet by four principles (adequacy, balance, moderation, diversity); the exact mix varies by person and culture, and it helps protect against malnutrition and diseases.

facts.text: WHO's healthy-diet fact sheet (updated January 2026) says the exact make-up of a healthy diet varies with individual characteristics, cultural context and locally available foods, while the basic principles stay the same.

WHO's four principles of a healthy diet: adequacy (meeting nutrient needs without exceeding them), balance (energy in matches energy used), moderation (limiting foods that may be harmful) and diversity (a wide variety of foods within and across food groups).
According to WHO, a healthy diet helps protect against malnutrition in all its forms and against noncommunicable diseases such as diabetes, heart disease, stroke and cancer.

title: WHO's diet numbers
description: WHO recommends at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day for people over 10, free sugars under 10 percent of daily energy and salt under 5 g a day.

facts.text: WHO recommends at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day for everyone older than 10, and at least 250 g for children aged 2 to 5 and 350 g for ages 6 to 9.
The NHS '5 A Day' campaign is based on WHO's 400 g advice; the NHS counts one portion of fruit or vegetables as 80 g, so five portions make 400 g.

WHO advises keeping free sugars under 10 percent of total daily energy intake; free sugars are sugars added by the manufacturer, cook or consumer, plus sugars naturally in honey, syrups and fruit juices.
WHO's free-sugars limit does not apply to the sugars in fresh fruit and vegetables or the sugars naturally present in milk.
WHO recommends adults eat less than 5 g of salt a day, just under a teaspoon.
The world's average salt intake is about 11 g a day, more than double WHO's recommended limit.
In many countries, most salt in the diet comes from processed foods such as ready meals, processed meats, bread, cheese and salty snacks.

title: WHO's 2020 physical activity guidelines
description: WHO's 2020 guidelines recommend an average of 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a day for ages 5 to 17 and 150 to 300 minutes a week for adults; the CDC's talk test tells moderate from vigorous.

facts.text: A WHO-led 2019 study of surveys covering 1.6 million students aged 11 to 17 found that 81 percent of adolescents worldwide were not active enough to meet WHO's recommendation.

WHO's 2020 guidelines recommend that children and adolescents aged 5 to 17 do an average of 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous, mostly aerobic activity, with vigorous activity and muscle- and bone-strengthening on at least 3 days a week.

WHO's 2020 guidelines recommend that adults aged 18 to 64 do 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week.
The CDC's talk test: during moderate-intensity activity you can talk but not sing; during vigorous activity you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath.

WHO's message is that any amount of physical activity is better than none and all of it counts, including walking, cycling, sports, active recreation and play, whether for leisure, getting around, work or chores.

title: What activity does for the body
description: Regular activity improves fitness, heart and bone health, thinking and mental health; for adults it lowers heart disease risk and improves sleep, and some brain benefits come right after a session.

facts.text: For children and adolescents, WHO lists benefits of physical activity including better heart, lung and muscle fitness, heart and metabolic health, bone health, thinking skills and mental health.
For adults, WHO lists benefits including lower risk of heart disease, high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes, better sleep, and fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression.
The CDC notes that some brain-health benefits of physical activity happen right after a session of moderate-to-vigorous activity.

title: How much sleep people need
description: CDC recommendations, based on AASM consensus statements, are 9 to 12 hours for ages 6 to 12, 8 to 10 for teens and 7 or more for adults; most US high schoolers get less than 8.

facts.text: In the CDC's 2025 youth survey, only 24 percent of US high school students got at least 8 hours of sleep on an average school night.

The CDC, drawing on American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus statements, recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep per 24 hours for ages 6 to 12, 8 to 10 hours for teens aged 13 to 17, and 7 or more hours for adults aged 18 to 60.

title: Why sleep matters for health
description: Sleep helps learning and long-term memory, supports growth in young people, helps immune defenses and gives the heart a rest; enough sleep is linked to lower risk of several chronic diseases.

facts.text: According to the NIH's National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, sleep helps with learning and the formation of long-term memories.
In children and teens, sleep also helps support growth and development.
Not getting enough sleep can cause problems focusing on tasks and thinking clearly.
During non-REM sleep, heart rate and blood pressure fall, so the heart does not work as hard.
Some immune cells work harder during sleep, and people who don't get enough sleep may be more likely to catch colds and other infections.
The CDC links getting enough sleep to lower risk of chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure and stroke.

title: The stress response
description: The amygdala alerts the hypothalamus; adrenaline speeds heart and breathing and releases stored fuel; cortisol keeps the body alert; the parasympathetic nervous system then acts as a brake.

facts.text: NIMH describes stress as the body's physical or mental response to an outside cause, such as a lot of homework or an illness.
The stress response can be set off by things that aren't life-threatening, such as traffic jams, work pressure and family difficulties.

When the eyes or ears sense danger, the amygdala sends a distress signal to the hypothalamus, which works like a command center for the stress response; this starts even before the brain's visual centers have fully processed what is happening.

In the stress response, adrenaline (epinephrine) makes the heart beat faster, pushing blood to the muscles, heart and other vital organs; breathing speeds up, small airways in the lungs open wide, and stored sugar and fat are released for energy.

As the adrenaline surge fades, a second hormone system (the HPA axis) keeps cortisol flowing to hold the body on alert; when the threat passes, cortisol falls and the parasympathetic nervous system acts as a brake that calms the response.
The American physiologist Walter Cannon described the fight-or-flight response and coined the phrase in the early 1900s.

title: Short-term and long-lasting stress
description: Short bursts of stress can help you meet a challenge, but stress that doesn't let up can affect sleep and several body systems; talking with a trusted adult or health professional can help.

facts.text: Short-term stress can be helpful, for example by pushing a person to meet a deadline.
Stress that lasts a long time can affect sleep and the immune, digestive, cardiovascular and reproductive systems.
Health guides from NIMH and Nemours KidsHealth say that when stress feels like too much or won't go away, talking with a trusted adult or a health professional can help.

title: Sunlight and vitamin D
description: Skin makes vitamin D from UVB in sunlight; vitamin D helps regulate calcium and phosphate for bones, teeth and muscles; glass blocks UVB, and winter sun in places like the UK is too weak.

facts.text: WHO says ultraviolet radiation in small amounts is essential to good health, because it leads to the production of vitamin D in the body.
The skin makes vitamin D when it is exposed to ultraviolet B (UVB) rays in sunlight.
Vitamin D helps regulate the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body, which are needed to keep bones, teeth and muscles healthy; a lack of it can lead to rickets in children.
Window glass blocks UVB, so the skin does not make vitamin D from sunlight coming through a window.

The NHS says people in the UK make vitamin D from sunlight from about late March or early April to the end of September, but not enough from October to early March; UK government advice is to consider a daily vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter.

title: Too much UV and sun protection
description: Too much UV damages DNA, causes sunburn and raises risks of skin cancer, cataracts and skin ageing; WHO advises protection at UV Index 3 or above, and the CDC recommends SPF 15+ broad-spectrum sunscreen.

facts.text: WHO lists DNA damage and sunburn among the short-term effects of too much ultraviolet radiation.
Over time, too much ultraviolet radiation raises the risk of skin cancers, cataracts in the eyes and premature skin ageing, and sunburns in childhood raise the risk of skin cancer later in life.
The CDC says any change in skin color after UV exposure, whether a tan or a burn, is a sign of injury, not health.
WHO says sun protection should be used when the UV Index reaches 3 or above: shade (especially around midday), protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses and broad-spectrum sunscreen.
The CDC recommends broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 15 or higher, reapplied after 2 hours in the sun and after swimming, sweating or toweling off.
WHO says sunscreen should not be used to extend the time spent in the sun.

title: Clinical-trial phases
description: New medicines go from preclinical lab tests to Phase 1 (safety and dose), Phase 2 (does it work, side effects), Phase 3 (large trials) and Phase 4 (monitoring after approval).

facts.text: Before a new drug is tested in people, preclinical research in the laboratory and in animals answers basic questions about its safety.

In FDA's description, Phase 1 tests safety and dosage in 20 to 100 people; Phase 2 tests efficacy and side effects in up to several hundred people with the condition; Phase 3 tests efficacy and watches for harms in 300 to 3,000 people over 1 to 4 years.
Phase 4 trials take place after a drug is approved, following several thousand people to keep checking its safety and effectiveness.

title: Placebos, randomization and blinding
description: Trials compare a medicine with an inactive placebo, assign people at random and often blind patients and doctors, so that expectation and chance can be told apart from the drug's real effect.

facts.text: The UK Medical Research Council's trial of streptomycin for tuberculosis, published in 1948, is widely regarded as the first randomized controlled trial; patients were allocated using random numbers kept in sealed envelopes that investigators could not see.
A placebo is an inactive substance that looks like the drug or treatment being tested.
The placebo effect is a beneficial health outcome that comes from a person's expectation that a treatment will help.
In randomized controlled trials, comparing a group given the treatment with a group given a placebo shows whether changes come from the treatment or occur by chance.
Random allocation stops investigators from choosing, consciously or unconsciously, which patients get the new treatment, which could bias the result.
In a blind test, patients don't know whether they got the real drug or a placebo; in a double-blind test, neither the patients nor their doctors know.

title: Anesthesia ends the agony
description: On 16 October 1846 in Boston, William Morton showed that ether could make surgery painless, so surgeons no longer had to operate at speed on patients who felt everything.

facts.text: The monument on William T. G. Morton's grave in Mount Auburn Cemetery calls him the man 'before whom in all time surgery was agony'.

On 16 October 1846 at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, the dentist William Morton gave ether to Edward Gilbert Abbott, a young housepainter, while a tumor was removed from his neck; Abbott reported feeling no pain, and the date became known as Ether Day.
Before anesthesia, patients felt the operation, so surgeons had to operate quickly; with ether, speed was no longer essential.

title: From antisepsis to asepsis
description: Joseph Lister used carbolic acid from 1865 to kill germs in wounds and on instruments; modern surgery aims for asepsis, sterilizing everything that touches the surgical field.

facts.text: Between 1861 and 1865, 45 to 50 percent of amputation patients in Joseph Lister's ward at Glasgow Royal Infirmary died from sepsis, an infection.

After learning of Louis Pasteur's germ theory, Joseph Lister concluded that microorganisms caused wound infections, and from 1865 he used carbolic acid to clean instruments and wounds; deaths in his ward fell sharply.
Asepsis means freedom from disease-causing germs; in aseptic surgery, all instruments and materials that touch the surgical field are sterilized, typically with steam under pressure in an autoclave.

In 1889 at Johns Hopkins, surgeon William Halsted had thin rubber gloves made for nurse Caroline Hampton, whose hands were damaged by harsh disinfectants; made to protect her skin, surgical gloves were later linked to fewer infections.

title: Rejection and matching
description: The immune system can attack a donated organ's foreign antigens; doctors match blood and tissue types, and recipients take immunosuppressants, usually for life. Identical twins match almost perfectly.

facts.text: Transplant rejection happens when the recipient's immune system attacks the donated organ, recognizing its cells by antigens, proteins on the cell surface that differ from the recipient's own.
No two people have identical tissue antigens except identical twins, whose tissues are genetically identical, so transplants between identical twins are almost never rejected.
Before a transplant, doctors check blood type (ABO typing) and tissue type (HLA typing) of donor and recipient; the closer the match, the lower the chance of rejection.

Most transplant recipients take immunosuppressant medicines for the rest of their lives to stop rejection; such drugs made possible the first successful kidney transplant from an unrelated donor, in 1962.

title: The first successful transplant
description: On 23 December 1954, Joseph Murray's team moved a kidney from Ronald Herrick to his identical twin Richard; today one donor can save up to 8 lives.

facts.text: To confirm that Richard and Ronald Herrick were identical twins, doctors ran 17 tests, including fingerprinting at a nearby police station.

On 23 December 1954 in Boston, Joseph Murray's team transplanted a kidney from Ronald Herrick into his identical twin Richard: the first successful human organ transplant. Richard lived eight more years.
From grafting skin during and after World War II, Joseph Murray had learned that tissue from an identical twin is not rejected.
Joseph Murray shared the 1990 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his transplant work.
One organ donor can save up to 8 lives, according to the US organ donation agency HRSA.
A living person can donate a kidney, because people can live with one kidney.

title: Body myths debunked
description: We use far more than 10 percent of our brains, every part of the tongue with taste buds senses all tastes, spiders avoid sleeping people, hair and nails don't grow after death and the head isn't a special heat leak.

facts.text: The idea that people use only 10 percent of their brains is a myth: brain imaging shows no area of the brain is completely silent, damage to almost any area has specific, lasting effects, and no 'unused 90 percent' has ever been found.

The tongue map is a myth: a 1901 study by David Hanig found only minute differences in taste sensitivity around the tongue, a 1940s redrawing by Edwin Boring turned it into separate zones, and in fact all areas with taste buds sense all tastes.
Swallowing spiders in your sleep is a myth: a sleeping person's heartbeat and breathing make vibrations that warn spiders away, and most spiders prefer quiet, secluded places.
Hair and nails don't grow after death, because growth needs hormonal control that stops; as the skin dries and pulls back, they only look longer.
The head is only about 10 percent of the body's surface, and heat loss roughly matches how much skin is uncovered, so the head is no special heat leak.

title: Testing myths with evidence
description: Donald Unger's 50-year one-hand experiment and a 2011 study found no link between knuckle cracking and arthritis; blinded trials show sugar doesn't make kids hyper, but expecting it changes what parents see.

facts.text: For 50 years, physician Donald Unger cracked the knuckles of his left hand at least twice a day and left his right hand as a control; he reported in 1998 that neither hand had arthritis, and won a 2009 Ig Nobel Prize.
A 2011 study of 215 people found hand osteoarthritis was about as common in habitual knuckle crackers as in people who don't crack their knuckles.
Double-blind trials have found that sugar does not affect children's behavior or thinking, as a 1995 JAMA meta-analysis concluded.
In a 1994 study, all the boys got a sugar-free placebo, but mothers told their sons had been given sugar rated them as more hyperactive.
